# What Is DataVo?

> Source route: /manual/preface/what-is-datavo
> Source file: manual/preface/what-is-datavo.md

DataVo is an embedded database engine written in C# for .NET 10. It runs inside your process: you create a `DataVoContext`, choose where the data lives, and run SQL or compiled LINQ against it. There is no server to deploy, no native library to load, and no wire protocol between your code and the storage engine.

The smallest DataVo program creates an in-memory database, defines a table, inserts a row, and reads it back.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE Demo");
db.Execute("USE Demo");

db.Execute("""
CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80)
);
""");

db.Execute("INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'Ada')");

var result = db.Execute("SELECT Id, Name FROM Users WHERE Id = 1")[0];
Console.WriteLine(result.Data[0]["Name"]);
```

For persisted data, the same API switches to the log-structured storage engine:

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

## Versions

The latest published NuGet packages are **0.4.0-rc.1** (17 November 2026), which ship both the **v0.3** and **v0.4** milestones described in this manual. The [Roadmap](/manual/preface/roadmap) lists what each milestone added and what v0.5 plans.

## How the engine is put together

DataVo has two storage engines that are under active development, and one legacy engine.

- **InMemory** keeps each table's rows in a packed row store (`FlatRowStore`): fixed-width cells in contiguous buffers rather than one object per row. An integer primary key is a hash map from key to row slot. For key ranges, the map builds a sorted copy of its keys on the first range query and keeps it current with a log of later inserts. Nothing survives the process.
- **LSM** is a log-structured merge tree. A write is appended to the data directory's commit log (`commit.wal`), applied to an arena-backed MemTable, and acknowledged; with `LsmStrictFsync = true` the acknowledgement waits for the log to reach stable storage. At 32 MB a MemTable is frozen and flushed by a background thread to an immutable SSTable, and SSTables are later merged by compaction. Tables whose primary key is a single `INT` or `GUID` column are clustered: rows are stored under their key, so a key lookup or a key range is a seek, not an index probe followed by a row fetch. SSTables are memory-mapped, secondary indexes are themselves keyed SSTables written in the same commit as the rows, and HNSW graphs are saved on close and caught up on open.
- **Disk** is the earlier paged file engine. It is kept so that existing data stays readable and receives no new work. Use LSM for persistent data.

On top of the storage engines sits one SQL implementation. A query is first offered to a set of **typed paths** that read cells directly from stored rows: a single-table scan, a hash join over integer keys, a columnar index, an index-driven join, and a vector-search planner. A typed path either produces exactly the result the general evaluator would, or declines. A query that no typed path accepts runs on the **general path**, which builds a dictionary per row and handles every supported construct, at a cost of kilobytes of allocation per row read. Most of DataVo's performance work is about widening the typed paths so that common queries never fall back. [Query Planner And Fast Paths](/manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths) lists what each path covers.

Vector columns (`VECTOR(n)`) are ordinary columns. A `FLAT` index compares the query with every stored vector using SIMD kernels; an `HNSW` index searches a navigable small-world graph and switches to an exact scan when a filtered query needs so many candidates that the scan is cheaper. Both answer `ORDER BY v <=> @q LIMIT k` in SQL, with or without filters and joins, so embeddings and the records they describe live in one engine and one transaction log.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Documents (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Title VARCHAR(200),
  Embedding VECTOR(1536)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_documents_embedding
ON Documents (Embedding)
USING HNSW;
```

## Ways to call it

| Package | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `DataVo.Core` | The engine and `DataVoContext`: SQL text, prepared statements, typed tables (`DataVoTable<T>`), reactive queries. |
| `DataVo.Generators` | A Roslyn source generator. `[DataVoQuery]` methods and `DataVoTable<T>` lambdas are compiled at build time into code that reads cells from the stored bytes. It has no dependency on Entity Framework Core and is Native AOT compatible. |
| `DataVo.Data` | An ADO.NET provider (`DbConnection`, `DbCommand`, `DbDataReader`), which also makes Dapper work. |
| `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` | A bridge that attaches DataVo storage to an EF Core context. It is not a standalone EF provider and has no migrations. |

`DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data` build with the trim and AOT analyzers as errors, so an application that uses them can be published with `PublishAot=true`. A browser build (`DataVo.Browser`) runs the engine in WebAssembly for this site's playground; it is not published on npm. [Choosing an Interface](/manual/getting-started/choosing-an-interface) compares the options.

## What DataVo is good at, and what it is not

DataVo was built for local-first .NET applications, game tooling, simulations, and retrieval workloads that keep embeddings next to relational data. On a single machine, with data in the operating system's page cache, the v0.4 engine is faster than SQLite on primary-key and secondary-index lookups, low-cardinality `GROUP BY`, inner and `LEFT` joins on integer keys, aggregates a columnar index can answer, and filtered vector search. SQLite is still faster on `GROUP BY` over a key it can read in index order, on full scans with `OR` or `LIKE`, and on an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`; DuckDB is one to three orders of magnitude faster than both on whole-table analytics. [DataVo vs SQLite](/manual/performance/datavo-vs-sqlite) gives the numbers and the reasons.

It is not a client/server database. One process owns a database directory at a time (`datavo.lock` enforces it), there is no network protocol, no replication, no stored procedures or triggers, and transactions do not provide serializable isolation for arbitrary multi-row predicates. Its SQL is its own dialect, not PostgreSQL's or SQLite's. The [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility), [Limits](/manual/reference/limits) and [Unsupported Features](/manual/reference/unsupported-features) state these boundaries precisely.

## Commercial Add-On: DataVo Sync

While DataVo itself is an MIT-licensed embedded database, teams needing **offline-first bidirectional synchronization with PostgreSQL** can license **DataVo Sync**, a separate proprietary commercial add-on. It connects PostgreSQL logical replication (`pgoutput`) to embedded DataVo clients over WebSocket/HTTP using wire v2 + Brotli, Z-set delta compaction, per-column conflict resolution, and crash-recoverable write-back.

In end-to-end Linux x64 CI benchmarks (20 November 2026, PostgreSQL 17.12, 2 vCPU):

- **100k warm initial sync:** **605 ms** (`InMemory`) and **706–726 ms** (`Lsm`) vs **702–909 ms** (SQLite/JSON) and **1,167 ms** (ElectricSQL `1.8.1`).
- **Wire footprint & allocations:** **45.5 B/row** (8.0× smaller than ElectricSQL's `362.7 B/row`) and **36.4–49.1 MB** client allocations (5.1–6.9× lower than ElectricSQL's `251.4 MB`).
- **Concurrency:** sustains **1,000 concurrent WebSocket clients** (`12,754 rows/s`) on a 2-vCPU VM, with **4.06–5.19 µs** local point lookups and **81–243 ms** offline-burst convergence across PostgreSQL and peers.

For licensing or early-access inquiries, reach out to `@ArintonAkos` on GitHub.

# Project Status & Stability

> Source route: /manual/preface/project-status
> Source file: manual/preface/project-status.md

**Latest published packages: 0.4.0-rc.1 (release candidate, 17 November 2026).**

DataVo is a C#-native embedded database engine. The **0.4.0-rc.1** packages on nuget.org ship the 0.2 baseline together with the completed **v0.3** (columnar indexes, compact in-memory rows) and **v0.4** (columnar SSTables, SQL and vector correctness, typed execution) milestones listed in the [Roadmap](/manual/preface/roadmap). This page says what "release candidate" promises and what state each subsystem is in.

## What "release candidate" means here

- The documented API surface and SQL dialect are the surface being verified. Changes to it are called out in release notes.
- Behaviour outside the documented surface is not covered. [Limits](/manual/reference/limits) and [Unsupported Features](/manual/reference/unsupported-features) list those boundaries.
- Packages are prereleases on nuget.org; add `--prerelease` when installing. See [Installation & Packages](/manual/getting-started/installation).
- The on-disk format is not covered by a long-term compatibility guarantee. v0.4 writes SSTable format version 8 and still reads the earlier row-keyed versions (2, 4 and 6), but there is no promise yet that a future version will read today's files. Keep a way to rebuild important data (an export, seed data or an import script).

## Subsystem status

| Subsystem | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embedded API (`DataVoContext`) | Release candidate | The primary interface. |
| SQL dialect (DDL, DML, queries) | Release candidate | DataVo's own dialect, not PostgreSQL-compatible. See the [compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility). |
| In-Memory storage | Release candidate | Ephemeral by design. |
| LSM-Tree storage | Release candidate | The recommended persistent engine: WAL, MemTable, SSTables, strict fsync by default. |
| Disk storage (paged) | Legacy | Kept for existing data. It receives no further durability work. Prefer LSM. |
| Transactions and MVCC | Release candidate | Snapshot isolation ordered by commit, read-your-own-writes across chained DML and savepoints, first-committer-wins conflicts, atomic `COMMIT`. Not serializable (write skew is possible). See [Transactions](/manual/storage-engine/transactions-acid-mvcc). |
| Compiled LINQ and source generators | Release candidate | Supported shapes are listed in [Roslyn Source Generators](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators). Other shapes still return the right rows by scanning. No Entity Framework dependency. |
| Vector search (HNSW and FLAT) | Release candidate | Cosine and L2 distance, filtered and joined searches with exact cost-based fallback, HNSW parameters in SQL (v0.4). See [Vector Search and Indexes](/manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax). |
| Columnar indexes | Release candidate (v0.3, persisted in v0.4) | In-memory column buffers; on LSM, columnar SSTable segments with zone maps. Included in `0.4.0-rc.1`. |
| ADO.NET provider (`DataVo.Data`) | Release candidate | Standard `System.Data.Common` types. See [ADO.NET Provider](/manual/client-interfaces/ado-net). |
| Dapper | Works through ADO.NET | No separate package. See [Dapper](/manual/client-interfaces/dapper). |
| Entity Framework Core integration | Bridge | Attaches DataVo to an EF context with a host EF provider. It is not a standalone provider and has no migrations. See [Entity Framework Core](/manual/client-interfaces/entity-framework). |
| Native AOT | Supported | `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data` build with the trim and AOT analyzers as errors. |
| Browser / WebAssembly (`DataVo.Browser`) | Experimental / Playground Lane | Interactive documentation playground (`docs/src/DataVoClient.ts`); not a production target and not published on npm. |
| PostgreSQL replication (DataVo-Sync) | Separate product | Not part of the NuGet packages. Proprietary replication bridge to PostgreSQL. |
| Unity | Evaluation target | See below. |

## Preview contracts

SQL `DATE` materializes as `DataVo.Core.DataVoDate` in the row APIs. `CellValue.AsDate()` and compiled `GetDate` return `DataVoDate`; modern .NET callers keep explicit `FromDateOnly`, `ToDateOnly`, `AsDateOnly` and `GetDateOnly` adapters. Existing persisted `DATE` bytes are unchanged.

## Unity Evaluation Status

Unity is an evaluation target, not a supported runtime. The public `DataVo.Core` package contains only a `net10.0` asset. `DataVoEnablePortableTarget=true` creates an experimental local `netstandard2.1` candidate only. A passing .NET-host verifier by itself is not Unity Editor, Mono, IL2CPP, Jobs, or Burst proof.

| Environment or boundary | Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unity 6000.5.4f1 Editor | Verified (narrow smoke) | The tracked project imports the generated candidate and its EditMode smoke suite passes. |
| macOS IL2CPP (6000.5.4f1) | Verified (narrow smoke) | A Medium-stripping Player builds, launches, performs the Unity type-binding scenario, writes a passing report, and exits zero. |
| Windows x64 IL2CPP | Unverified | Windows requires its own built-and-executed Player proof. |
| Direct Burst calls | Unsupported by design | DataVo uses managed engine types and services and is not a Burst job payload. |
| Job-to-managed batch bridge | Planned proof | A Burst-compatible job may produce POD commands that managed code drains after completion. |
| In-memory mode | Candidate scope | This is the only storage mode included in the Stage 3 Unity candidate proof. |
| Disk/LSM persistence | Verified (narrow smoke) | Save, close and reopen pass for both modes in the Unity 6000.5.4f1 macOS Editor and a macOS IL2CPP Player. Other platforms and power-loss behaviour are unverified. |

## Scope summary

| Feature | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-process embedded deployment | Supported | The core product shape is library-first, not server-first. |
| Public curated manual | Supported | The manual is the public documentation boundary. |
| SQL execution through `DataVoContext` | Supported | Core SQL commands and query forms are documented. |
| ADO.NET provider | Supported | `DataVoConnection`, `DataVoCommand`, `DataVoDataReader`; Dapper works through it. |
| Entity Framework bridge | Supported | Basic `DbSet` workflows and query previews with explicit operator limits, not a full provider. |
| Roslyn source generators | Supported | `[DataVoQuery]` and typed table queries compile at build time. |
| NuGet packaging | Supported | Four packages. The public Core package is `net10.0`-only; the opt-in portable target is an experimental local candidate, not a published or supported Unity asset. Multi-target packages are planned for v0.5. |
| Stable storage format | Planned | Requires compatibility tests and migration guidance. |
| Production support contract | Not Supported | No production support contract is offered. |
| Stored procedures, triggers, PostgreSQL-compatible server | Not Supported | See [Unsupported Features](/manual/reference/unsupported-features). |

# Release Scope & Boundaries

> Source route: /manual/preface/alpha-scope
> Source file: manual/preface/alpha-scope.md

This page states the contract: what DataVo is built to do, the settings under which its guarantees hold, and what it deliberately does not do. It applies to the v0.4 line published as **0.4.0-rc.1** (17 November 2026); see the [Roadmap](/manual/preface/roadmap) for the milestone breakdown and [Project Status & Stability](/manual/preface/project-status) for the state of each subsystem.

## The supported shape

One .NET 10 process opens a database directory (or an in-memory database), executes SQL or compiled LINQ through `DataVoContext`, ADO.NET, or the EF Core bridge, and closes it.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./app_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App");
db.Execute("USE App");
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE Events (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80))");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'created')");
```

Within that shape:

- **Durability.** With `StorageMode.Lsm` and `LsmStrictFsync = true` (the default), a commit is acknowledged only after its commit-log record has been flushed to stable storage, so an acknowledged write survives a crash or power loss, provided the drive honours flushes. With `LsmStrictFsync = false` the record is handed to the operating system and the acknowledgement does not wait: a process crash loses nothing the OS has accepted, but a power failure or kernel crash can lose the most recent commits. [WAL And Durability](/manual/storage-engine/wal-and-durability) has the details.
- **Isolation.** Explicit transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`) buffer their writes until commit, readers see MVCC snapshots, and updates and deletes revalidate rows before modifying them. Serializability across arbitrary multi-row predicates is not provided: a transaction that reads "all active users" can miss a row another transaction inserts. See [Transactions and MVCC](/manual/storage-engine/transactions-acid-mvcc).
- **Query results.** Every typed fast path returns exactly the result of the general SQL evaluator, or declines. Vector search with `FLAT` is exact; `HNSW` is approximate unless the planner routes the query to an exact scan, and its recall depends on the data. The SQL dialect is DataVo's own; the [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility) lists what it accepts.
- **Native AOT.** `DataVo.Core`, `DataVo.Data` and code generated by `DataVo.Generators` publish with `PublishAot=true` without trim or AOT warnings. `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` is not covered, because EF Core itself is not.

## Boundaries

| Area | Status | What that means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Multiple processes on one database directory | Not supported | `datavo.lock` rejects a second process. Contexts in one process share one engine. |
| Serializable isolation, phantom prevention | Not supported | No predicate or range locks. |
| Network access, PostgreSQL wire protocol | Not supported | Embedded only. A `DataVo.Server` bridge is planned but unscheduled. |
| Stored procedures, triggers, user-defined functions | Not supported | Keep that logic in application code. |
| Replication, high availability | Out of scope | |
| EF Core migrations, shadow properties, complex LINQ joins | Not supported | The EF integration is a bridge, not a provider. |
| `StorageMode.Disk` | Legacy | Readable for existing data; receives no durability or performance work. Use `Lsm`. |
| Long-term on-disk format guarantee | Not yet | Keep seed data or an export path until a stable release states one. |
| Browser / WebAssembly (`DataVo.Browser`) | Playground only | Powers this site's playground; not production-ready and not on npm. |
| Unity | Evaluation target | Narrow Editor and macOS IL2CPP smoke only; see [Unity evaluation status](/manual/preface/project-status#unity-evaluation-status). |

## SQL DATE contract

SQL `DATE` materializes as `DataVo.Core.DataVoDate` in the row APIs. `CellValue.AsDate()` and compiled `GetDate` return `DataVoDate`; on modern .NET, `FromDateOnly`, `ToDateOnly`, `AsDateOnly` and `GetDateOnly` convert explicitly to and from `System.DateOnly`. Persisted `DATE` bytes are unchanged by this API.

---

# Roadmap

> Source route: /manual/preface/roadmap
> Source file: manual/preface/roadmap.md

DataVo's milestones are numbered by what they change in the engine. The latest published NuGet packages are **0.4.0-rc.1**, which ship both **v0.3** and **v0.4**; **v0.5** is planned next. The principles behind every milestone are the same: one process owns its data, durability is an explicit setting with a stated contract, `DataVo.Core` stays Native AOT clean, and a fast path either returns exactly what the general path would or declines.

## v0.2: the embedded engine (first 0.2.0-rc.3 line)

- **LSM storage.** A commit log, arena-backed MemTables, background SSTable flushes and compaction. `LsmStrictFsync = true` (the default) acknowledges a commit only after the log is on stable storage. Tables whose primary key is one `INT` or `GUID` column are clustered: rows are stored under their key, which roughly halves the footprint of an integer-keyed table compared with a separate primary-key index.
- **Native AOT.** `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data` build with the trim and AOT analyzers (`IL2026`, `IL3050`) as errors.
- **Allocation-free reads.** In-memory primary-key lookups that skip SQL parsing and row dictionaries, and `StreamRef()`/`RowRef` table scans that allocate nothing.
- **Vector search.** `VECTOR(n)` columns, `HNSW` and `FLAT` indexes, cosine (`<=>`) and Euclidean (`<->`) distance with SIMD kernels.
- **Packaging.** `DataVo.Core`, `DataVo.Data`, `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` and `DataVo.Generators` on nuget.org as prereleases, published from CI with NuGet Trusted Publishing.

## v0.3: columnar indexes and compact rows (shipped in 0.4.0-rc.1)

- **Columnar indexes** (`[Columnar]` on a typed model, `CREATE INDEX ... USING COLUMNAR` in SQL). The marked columns are kept a second time as contiguous column buffers, and single-table `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` with numeric `AND`/`OR` filters are answered from those buffers with SIMD kernels instead of from rows.
- **Compact in-memory rows.** `FlatRowStore` packs rows into fixed-width cells in contiguous buffers, read through `PackedKeyReader<T>`: 49.2 bytes per row in the measured table, 13 times less than the previous object-per-row layout, and a 52.1 ns primary-key lookup.

## v0.4: out-of-core columns, SQL and vector correctness, typed execution (published as 0.4.0-rc.1)

v0.4 makes the LSM engine's columnar data persistent, fixes every wrong answer a cross-engine oracle found, and moves the common SQL shapes onto typed paths. Its final measurements are in [`2026-11-16-v04-final/`](https://github.com/ArintonAkos/DataVo-DBMS/tree/master/docs/public/benchmarks/2026-11-16-v04-final) and explained in [DataVo vs SQLite](/manual/performance/datavo-vs-sqlite).

**Storage**

- **Columnar SSTables (format version 8).** Flush and compaction write the columnar index's columns into each `.sst` file as 4,096-row segments, with NULL and NaN masks, runs of deleted keys, and a min/max zone map per chunk. Only the unflushed tail of a table is held in memory, so opening a database does not rebuild the index, and a scan skips any chunk whose zone map rules out the predicate. Compaction merges segments as a stream instead of materializing them.
- **Shadow masks and delete vectors.** A row in an SSTable segment can be replaced or deleted by a newer file or by the unflushed tail. Each SSTable keeps a delete vector, a bit per row for the chunks that have such rows, built for one set of live files and extended incrementally when the set changes; the rows the tail shadows are marked per scan in a reused mask that grows as the tail grows. A columnar scan therefore never counts a replaced or deleted row.

**Correctness.** A benchmark that checks every answer against an oracle before timing it found five queries on which DataVo returned a wrong result. All five are fixed, with regression tests on both active engines; [Correctness findings](/manual/performance/datavo-vs-sqlite#correctness-findings) describes each.

- `B1`: a `WHERE` condition on the NULL-supplying side of a `LEFT JOIN` was applied before the join.
- `B2`: `DISTINCT` inside an aggregate (`COUNT(DISTINCT x)`) was dropped by the parser.
- `B3`: a filtered vector search over aliased tables fetched too few candidates.
- `B4`: `AND`/`OR` across two joined tables intersected row keys listed in different table orders.
- `B5`: a vector search joined to another table dropped the joined table's filter.
- `WHERE ... HAVING` without `GROUP BY` failed to parse; `HAVING` now ends the `WHERE` condition.
- A `BIT` column could not be filtered: `WHERE IsActive = true` failed to bind, and `= 1` or `= 'true'` silently matched no row. `TRUE`/`FALSE`, `1`/`0` and `'true'`/`'false'` now all compare as booleans.
- On the legacy Disk engine, an indexed `DOUBLE` equality found no row under a culture whose decimal separator is a comma, because the lookup key was formatted in that culture.

**Typed SQL execution**

- `OR` and `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE` on the typed single-table scan and on columnar indexes.
- A typed hash join for `INNER` and `LEFT` joins on integer keys over any number of tables, aggregated or returning rows, with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` kept to a bounded top-N.
- Index-driven joins: when a selective dimension names few rows of a large table, the large table is read through its index on the join column.
- A joined table that contributes only its key (an anti-join such as `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE c.Id IS NULL`) is kept as a dense bit set when its keys are distinct and closely spaced, instead of a hash table.
- `GROUP BY` without boxing its keys, with `HAVING`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` applied to the groups before any group becomes a row.
- On the LSM engine, text equality and `LIKE` are tested against the stored UTF-8 bytes rather than a decoded string per row.
- `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` without an index compares sort keys in place and copies only rows that enter the top-k.
- Primary-key ranges on the InMemory engine are read from the key map's sorted key copy.

**Vector search**

- HNSW's neighbour-selection diversity heuristic is on by default, and connectivity repair no longer drops the last edge into a cluster. On strongly clustered embeddings this raised recall@10 from 82–94% to 100%.
- HNSW answers a search by an exact scan when the candidate count a filter requires makes the graph walk more expensive. The scan is exact, so recall can only rise.
- A filtered vector search tests the `WHERE` conditions on the stored candidate rows and builds only the rows that pass; over a join, candidates go through the typed join and joined tables are read by key.
- `CREATE INDEX ... USING HNSW WITH (m, ef_construction, ef_search, enable_diversity_heuristic)` sets the graph parameters from SQL and stores them in the catalog.
- The SIMD distance kernels and the Flat scan loop are compiled fully optimized on first use. Under tiered compilation the first searches of a process, sometimes a whole run, used unoptimized kernel code: 11–14 ms instead of about 2 ms for an exact search over 50,000 × 384 vectors.

## v0.5: interop and client-side ergonomics (planned)

v0.5 has two tracks. The first item of Track B is done; the rest is the plan, not a commitment to dates.

**Track A: native interop.**

- A C ABI exported from a Native AOT build of the engine (`dv_open`, `dv_close`, `dv_exec`, `dv_prepare`, parameter binding, `dv_exec_prepared`, and a direct single-row read), so that C, Python, Rust or Go can embed DataVo without .NET.
- Zero-copy export of columnar data through the Apache Arrow C Data Interface (`ArrowArray`, `ArrowSchema`), from in-memory column buffers and from SSTable segments, for Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB and similar consumers.
- A reference Python binding with an end-to-end test and benchmark.

**Track B: client applications.**

- **Done:** more of LINQ compiled at build time by `DataVo.Generators`, still with no Entity Framework dependency: `OrderBy`/`OrderByDescending`/`ThenBy`/`ThenByDescending`, `Skip`/`Take`, `Select` projections that read only the projected columns, and compiled single-table `ExecuteDelete` and `ExecuteUpdate`. See [Roslyn Source Generators](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators#sorting-and-paging).
- Two-dimensional geographic data: WGS84 latitude/longitude points with spherical (haversine) distance, bounding boxes that cross the ±180° meridian, and a 2D spatial index (R-tree, quadtree or a Morton-ordered B-tree) so that radius and box queries over a million points do not scan the table. The current spatial support is three-dimensional Cartesian (`Vector3`) and scans.
- Multi-target packages (`net8.0`, `net9.0`, `net10.0`, and `netstandard2.1` where the code allows), so that MAUI, Avalonia, WPF, WinUI, Unity and Blazor WebAssembly applications are not blocked by a `net10.0`-only asset, and a guide for migrating client applications from `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` and EF Core.

## Later, and out of scope

| Item | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL wire protocol bridge (`DataVo.Server`) | Planned, unscheduled | A companion process speaking a subset of the PostgreSQL protocol so that DBeaver, DataGrip or pgAdmin can inspect a database directory. |
| Long-term on-disk format guarantee | Planned | Needs a cross-version compatibility suite and migration tooling. Until then, keep a way to rebuild important data. |
| Unity runtime support | Evaluation target | A narrow Editor and macOS IL2CPP smoke passes on Unity 6000.5.4f1; Windows IL2CPP is unverified and Burst is unsupported by design. |
| Browser / WebAssembly package (`DataVo.Browser`) | Playground only | Runs this site's playground; not published on npm. |
| EF Core migrations | Not planned | `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` is a query and DML bridge. |
| Replication and high availability | Out of scope | DataVo is an embedded engine. |

---

# Installation & Packages

> Source route: /manual/getting-started/installation
> Source file: manual/getting-started/installation.md

DataVo ships as four NuGet packages. Install only the ones you need: `DataVo.Core` is the engine and everything else builds on it.

The latest published packages are **0.4.0-rc.1 (release candidate)**, so include `--prerelease` when you add a package. They include the v0.3 and v0.4 features described in this manual; to build packages locally from this repository instead, run `dotnet pack DataVo.sln -c Release`, which writes them to `artifacts/packages`, and add that folder as a package source. See [Project Status & Stability](/manual/preface/project-status) for what that means.

## Packages

| Package | Install it when you want | What it adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DataVo.Core` | The embedded engine and SQL through `DataVoContext`. | Parser, planner, storage engines (In-Memory, LSM-Tree, legacy Disk), vector indexes, typed table API. |
| `DataVo.Data` | An ADO.NET provider, or a micro-ORM such as Dapper. | `DataVoConnection`, `DataVoCommand`, `DataVoDataReader`, `DataVoTransaction`, `DataVoParameter`. |
| `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` | An EF Core `DbContext` over DataVo. | `UseDataVo(...)`, `DataVoDbContext`, query-translation diagnostics. |
| `DataVo.Generators` | Compiled LINQ queries and `[DataVoQuery]` methods. | A Roslyn source generator and analyzer. It is a build-time reference, not a runtime dependency. |

```bash
dotnet add package DataVo.Core --prerelease
dotnet add package DataVo.Data --prerelease
dotnet add package DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore --prerelease
dotnet add package DataVo.Generators --prerelease
```

## Which packages for which job

| Job | Packages |
| --- | --- |
| Embedded SQL and the typed table API | `DataVo.Core` |
| Compiled LINQ scans and aggregates | `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Generators` |
| ADO.NET or Dapper | `DataVo.Data` (brings `DataVo.Core`) |
| EF Core | `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` (brings `DataVo.Core`) |

## Requirements

- **.NET 10.** The published `DataVo.Core` package contains a `net10.0` asset only. Other targets, including Unity, are not supported. See [Project Status](/manual/preface/project-status#unity-evaluation-status).
- **Native AOT** is supported by `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data`. See [Native AOT Deployment](/manual/client-interfaces/native-aot).
- **C# interceptors** are used by `DataVo.Generators`. The package's build props register the `DataVo.Generated` interceptors namespace for you, so no manual `InterceptorsNamespaces` entry is needed.

## Verify the install

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig { StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory });
db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE Smoke");
db.Execute("USE Smoke");
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE T (Id INT PRIMARY KEY)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO T (Id) VALUES (1)");

Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT Id FROM T")[0].Data.Count); // 1
```

Continue with the [Quickstart](/manual/tutorial/quickstart), or pick an API in [Choosing an Interface](/manual/getting-started/choosing-an-interface). See also [Project Status & Scope](/manual/preface/project-status).

---

# Choosing an Interface

> Source route: /manual/getting-started/choosing-an-interface
> Source file: manual/getting-started/choosing-an-interface.md

DataVo has five ways to talk to the same engine. They differ in ergonomics and in how much work happens per call, not in what the database can store. You can mix them in one application.

## Decision table

| Interface | Package | Best for | Per-call cost | Native AOT |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Compiled LINQ](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators) | `DataVo.Core` + `DataVo.Generators` | Hot paths: point lookups, filtered counts and aggregates. No EF Core dependency. | Lowest. Predicates are compiled at build time; aggregates allocate nothing once warm. | Yes |
| [Embedded API](/manual/client-interfaces/datavo-context-api) (`DataVoContext`) | `DataVo.Core` | Application code that wants SQL, DDL, vector search and full control. | Parses SQL per call unless prepared. Rows come back as dictionaries. | Yes |
| [ADO.NET provider](/manual/client-interfaces/ado-net) | `DataVo.Data` | Code or libraries that already speak `DbConnection`. | Same engine as the embedded API, behind the standard ADO.NET types. | Yes |
| [Dapper](/manual/client-interfaces/dapper) | `DataVo.Data` + `Dapper` | Micro-ORM mapping with plain SQL. | ADO.NET cost plus Dapper's mapping. | Per Dapper's own support |
| [Entity Framework Core](/manual/client-interfaces/entity-framework) | `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` | Existing EF models and `DbContext` workflows. | Highest. EF infrastructure sits on top of the engine. | Not claimed |

A short rule of thumb:

- Start with the **embedded API** to learn the engine and for anything that is not performance critical.
- Move the few queries that run constantly to **compiled LINQ**.
- Use **ADO.NET or Dapper** when you are adapting existing code or want a familiar abstraction.
- Use **EF Core** when the rest of your application is already modelled in EF. If you want LINQ without EF (for example under Native AOT), use compiled LINQ: `DataVo.Generators` has no EF dependency.

## How they fit together

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  App["Your application"]
  App --> LINQ["Compiled LINQ<br/>(DataVo.Generators)"]
  App --> Ctx["DataVoContext<br/>(DataVo.Core)"]
  App --> Ado["ADO.NET provider<br/>(DataVo.Data)"]
  App --> EF["EF Core integration<br/>(DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore)"]
  Dapper["Dapper"] --> Ado
  LINQ --> Core["DataVo.Core engine"]
  Ctx --> Core
  Ado --> Core
  EF --> Core
  Core --> Storage["In-Memory | LSM-Tree | Disk (legacy)"]
```

Every route ends in the same parser, planner and storage engines, so storage modes, durability settings and vector indexes behave identically whichever interface you use.

## The same question, five ways

"How many players are level 10 or higher?" The table is `players (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Level INT)`.

**Embedded API**

```csharp
var result = db.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) AS Total FROM players WHERE Level >= 10")[0];
object total = result.Data[0]["Total"];
```

**ADO.NET**

```csharp
using var cmd = connection.CreateCommand();
cmd.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM players WHERE Level >= @min";
cmd.Parameters.AddWithValue("@min", 10);
object? total = cmd.ExecuteScalar();
```

**Dapper**

```csharp
int total = connection.ExecuteScalar<int>(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM players WHERE Level >= @min", new { min = 10 });
```

**Entity Framework Core**

```csharp
List<Player> matches = context.QueryFromDataVo<Player>(query =>
    query.Where(static p => p.Level >= 10));
int total = matches.Count;
```

**Compiled LINQ**

```csharp
int total = db.Table<Player>().Where(10, static (p, min) => p.Level >= min).Count();
```

The compiled form reads the `Level` cell straight from the stored bytes and builds no `Player` objects. That is the mechanism behind the zero-allocation aggregates described in [Compiled Scan Kernels](/manual/internals/compiled-scan-kernels).

## Related

- [Installation & Packages](/manual/getting-started/installation)
- [ADO.NET & Dapper tutorial](/manual/tutorial/ado-net-and-dapper)
- [Benchmark Results](/manual/performance/benchmarks), to see what each approach costs in practice.

# Quickstart

> Source route: /manual/tutorial/quickstart
> Source file: manual/tutorial/quickstart.md

This quickstart creates a DataVo database entirely in memory. It is the fastest way to learn the API because it does not write files and it does not require a server.

Create a new console application and add the DataVo package when it is available from your package source. In the repository, use the project references or local package artifacts used by the solution.

```bash
dotnet new console -n DataVoQuickstart
cd DataVoQuickstart
dotnet add package DataVo.Core
```

Create a `DataVoContext` with `StorageMode.InMemory`.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.Contracts.Results;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});
```

DataVo can host multiple logical databases. Create one and make it the active database for the current session.

```csharp
db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE Demo");
db.Execute("USE Demo");
```

Define a table with a primary key and a few scalar columns.

```csharp
db.Execute("""
CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  Score FLOAT,
  IsActive BIT
);
""");
```

Insert a row. Column-targeted inserts are easier to maintain than full-row inserts because the column order is visible at the call site.

```csharp
db.Execute("""
INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (1, 'Ada', 98.5, true);
""");
```

Read the row back with ordinary SQL. `Execute` returns a list because a SQL string can contain multiple statements.

```csharp
List<QueryResult> results = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true
ORDER BY Score DESC
LIMIT 10;
""");

QueryResult result = results[0];

foreach (Dictionary<string, object?> row in result.Data)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{row["Id"]}: {row["Name"]} scored {row["Score"]}");
}
```

The same flow works with persistent LSM storage. Use strict LSM mode when you want writes to wait for WAL durability.

```csharp
using var persistentDb = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

Here is the full quickstart as one file.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.Contracts.Results;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE Demo");
db.Execute("USE Demo");

db.Execute("""
CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  Score FLOAT,
  IsActive BIT
);
""");

db.Execute("""
INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (1, 'Ada', 98.5, true);
""");

List<QueryResult> results = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true
ORDER BY Score DESC
LIMIT 10;
""");

foreach (Dictionary<string, object?> row in results[0].Data)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{row["Id"]}: {row["Name"]} scored {row["Score"]}");
}

// Output:
// 1: Ada scored 98.5
```

Expected output:

```text
1: Ada scored 98.5
```

## Quickstart Support

Everything in this quickstart is part of the public subset: constructing `DataVoContext` with a `DataVoConfig` (which selects storage mode and durability), `CREATE DATABASE` and `USE`, `CREATE TABLE` with primary keys and scalar columns, column-targeted `INSERT` (the value count must match the column list), and `SELECT ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT`. The general query API returns `QueryResult`; a strongly typed general API is planned, and source generators already provide typed calls for narrow shapes.

---

# Using DataVoContext

> Source route: /manual/tutorial/datavo-context
> Source file: manual/tutorial/datavo-context.md

`DataVoContext` is the main embedded API. It owns the engine instance, the default session, and the storage configuration for the process. Most applications start with one context per embedded database lifecycle.

Create a context with explicit configuration. During development, in-memory mode keeps setup simple.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.Contracts.Results;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});
```

Every statement runs in a logical session. If you call `Execute(sql)` without a session ID, DataVo uses the context's default session.

```csharp
db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App");
db.Execute("USE App");
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE Events (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80))");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'started')");
```

Read results through `QueryResult`. The general SQL path returns dictionaries keyed by column name.

```csharp
QueryResult result = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Name
FROM Events
ORDER BY Id ASC;
""")[0];

foreach (var row in result.Data)
{
    int id = Convert.ToInt32(row["Id"]);
    string name = Convert.ToString(row["Name"]) ?? "";
    Console.WriteLine($"{id}: {name}");
}
```

Use explicit sessions when you need independent transaction scopes. A transaction started in one session does not belong to another session.

```csharp
Guid writerSession = Guid.NewGuid();

db.Execute("USE App", writerSession);
db.Execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION", writerSession);
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name) VALUES (2, 'queued')", writerSession);
db.Execute("COMMIT", writerSession);
```

Rollback uses the same session-bound pattern.

```csharp
Guid rollbackSession = Guid.NewGuid();

db.Execute("USE App", rollbackSession);
db.Execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION", rollbackSession);
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name) VALUES (3, 'temporary')", rollbackSession);
db.Execute("ROLLBACK", rollbackSession);
```

For persistent storage, the context configuration is the only part that changes. Disk mode is the simpler file-backed backend.

```csharp
using var diskDb = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Disk,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_data",
    WalEnabled = true,
    SyncDiskWrites = true
});
```

LSM mode is the high-throughput backend. Keep `LsmStrictFsync = true` for durability-sensitive tests.

```csharp
using var lsmDb = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

## DataVoContext API Summary

`DataVoContext` supports `Execute(string query)` against the default session and `Execute(string query, Guid sessionId)` against an explicit session, session-bound transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`), dictionary row results in `QueryResult.Data`, and persistent `Disk` and `Lsm` storage (with WAL and durability settings). The public examples use synchronous `Execute`; an async general SQL API is planned.

---

# ADO.NET & Dapper Tutorial

> Source route: /manual/tutorial/ado-net-and-dapper
> Source file: manual/tutorial/ado-net-and-dapper.md

This tutorial builds a small player store through the ADO.NET provider, then reads it back with Dapper. It uses LSM storage, so the data survives a restart. Reference details live in [ADO.NET Provider](/manual/client-interfaces/ado-net) and [Dapper](/manual/client-interfaces/dapper).

## 1. Create a project

```bash
dotnet new console -n PlayerStore
cd PlayerStore
dotnet add package DataVo.Data --prerelease
dotnet add package Dapper
```

## 2. Open a persistent database

```csharp
using Dapper;
using DataVo.Data;

using var connection = new DataVoConnection("StorageMode=Lsm;DataSource=./player-store");
connection.Open();
```

`StorageMode=Lsm` selects the LSM-Tree engine with strict fsync by default. `DataSource` is both the data directory and the database name. See [Configuration Reference](/manual/reference/configuration).

## 3. Create the schema

```csharp
connection.Execute(
    "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Players (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(40), Level INT)");
```

## 4. Insert in a transaction

```csharp
using (var transaction = connection.BeginTransaction())
{
    for (int id = 1; id <= 5; id++)
    {
        connection.Execute(
            "INSERT INTO Players (Id, Name, Level) VALUES (@Id, @Name, @Level)",
            new { Id = id, Name = $"player-{id}", Level = id * 3 },
            transaction);
    }

    transaction.Commit();
}
```

Run the program twice: the second run fails on the primary key, which is the point. The rows from the first run were persisted.

## 5. Query with Dapper

```csharp
IEnumerable<Player> veterans = connection.Query<Player>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Level >= @min ORDER BY Level DESC",
    new { min = 9 });

foreach (Player p in veterans)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.Name}: level {p.Level}");
}

public sealed class Player
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public int Level { get; set; }
}
```

## 6. Drop to raw ADO.NET when you want to

Dapper and plain ADO.NET share the connection, so you can use either per call.

```csharp
using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Players WHERE Level >= @min";
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@min", 9);
Console.WriteLine(command.ExecuteScalar());
```

## Where to go next

- Move a hot query to [compiled LINQ](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators).
- Use [vector search](/manual/tutorial/vector-search-example) for embeddings in the same database.
- Read [WAL & Durability](/manual/storage-engine/wal-and-durability) before relying on persisted data.

---

# Entity Framework Example

> Source route: /manual/tutorial/entity-framework-example
> Source file: manual/tutorial/entity-framework-example.md

DataVo's Entity Framework Core integration (`DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore`) is a preview bridge. It lets you keep a familiar EF model while evaluating DataVo-backed persistence and DataVo-native query paths with explicit operator limits. It is not a standalone migration-capable EF provider.

Start with a mapped entity. Keep the first model simple: an integer key, a string column, and a boolean flag.

```csharp
public sealed class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public bool IsActive { get; set; }
}
```

Create a context that derives from `DataVoDbContext`. The example uses EF Core's in-memory provider as the host provider and then attaches DataVo with `UseDataVo`.

```csharp
using DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

public sealed class AppDbContext : DataVoDbContext
{
    public AppDbContext(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext> options)
        : base(options)
    {
    }

    public DbSet<User> Users => Set<User>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        modelBuilder.Entity<User>(entity =>
        {
            entity.ToTable("Users");
            entity.HasKey(static user => user.Id);
            entity.Property(static user => user.Name).HasMaxLength(80);
            entity.Property(static user => user.IsActive);
        });
    }
}
```

Build the options once and pass them into the context.

```csharp
var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
    .UseInMemoryDatabase("datavo-ef-host")
    .UseDataVo(dataVo => dataVo
        .UseInMemoryStorage()
        .WithDataSource("EfDemo"))
    .Options;
```

Insert through EF with `Add` and `SaveChanges`.

```csharp
using var writer = new AppDbContext(options);

writer.Database.EnsureCreated();

writer.Users.Add(new User
{
    Id = 1,
    Name = "Ada",
    IsActive = true
});

writer.SaveChanges();
```

Query with ordinary LINQ for supported LINQ operators.

```csharp
List<User> activeUsers = writer.Users
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(static user => user.Name)
    .ToList();
```

If a separate context needs to read data that already exists in DataVo, call `LoadFromDataVo` before querying.

```csharp
using var reader = new AppDbContext(options);

reader.LoadFromDataVo();

List<User> activeUsers = reader.Users
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .ToList();
```

For DataVo-native query evaluation, use `QueryFromDataVo`. This path validates the LINQ expression and keeps unsupported operators explicit.

```csharp
List<User> firstTen = reader.QueryFromDataVo<User>(query => query
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(static user => user.Id)
    .Take(10));
```

Vector queries use DataVo's EF function shims inside a supported DataVo-native query.

```csharp
float[] queryVector = [1f, 0f, 0f];

List<ItemEmbedding> nearest = ctx.QueryFromDataVo<ItemEmbedding>(query => query
    .Where(item => DataVoVectorDbFunctions.CosineDistance(EF.Functions, item.Vector, queryVector) < 0.3)
    .OrderBy(item => DataVoVectorDbFunctions.CosineDistance(EF.Functions, item.Vector, queryVector))
    .Take(5));
```

## EF Core Example Support

The bridge supports basic mapped `DbSet` querying, basic inserts via `Add` plus `SaveChanges`, `LoadFromDataVo` (refresh EF state before LINQ), `QueryFromDataVo` for supported LINQ query patterns, and vector function shims (`CosineDistance`, `L2Distance`) for preview translation. It does **not** support EF migrations, shadow properties, or complex provider-style LINQ joins.

---

# Vector Search Example

> Source route: /manual/tutorial/vector-search-example
> Source file: manual/tutorial/vector-search-example.md

This tutorial uses `DataVoContext` to create a tiny vector dataset and run nearest-neighbor queries. The example uses three-dimensional vectors so the data is readable, but the SQL shape is the same for production embeddings such as `VECTOR(1536)`.

Create an in-memory context and select a database.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.Contracts.Results;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE Vectors");
db.Execute("USE Vectors");
```

Create a table with a vector column.

```csharp
db.Execute("""
CREATE TABLE Embeddings (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Label VARCHAR(80),
  Emb VECTOR(3)
);
""");
```

Insert a few vectors. DataVo accepts bracketed numeric vector literals.

```csharp
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb) VALUES (1, 'red', '[1,0,0]')");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb) VALUES (2, 'green', '[0,1,0]')");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb) VALUES (3, 'warm-red', '[0.9,0.1,0]')");
```

Create a vector index. `FLAT` is exact and easy to reason about for small datasets.

```csharp
db.Execute("CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_flat ON Embeddings (Emb) USING FLAT");
```

Run a cosine-distance query. Lower distance values are closer.

```csharp
QueryResult cosine = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 3;
""")[0];

foreach (Dictionary<string, object?> row in cosine.Data)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{row["Label"]}: {row["distance"]}");
}
```

Expected output:

```text
red: 0
warm-red: 0.006116...
green: 1
```

Run the same query with L2 distance when Euclidean distance is the right measure for the embedding space.

```csharp
QueryResult l2 = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <-> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 3;
""")[0];
```

For larger tables, create an HNSW index instead. HNSW is approximate: it walks a neighbour graph instead of comparing the query with every vector, so it can miss a true neighbour, and how often depends on the data. The defaults (`m = 16`, `ef_construction = 64`, `ef_search = 64`, diversity heuristic on) are a reasonable start; `WITH (...)` changes them, as described in [Vector Search and Indexes](/manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax). Measure recall on your own embeddings before relying on it.

```csharp
db.Execute("CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_hnsw ON Embeddings (Emb) USING HNSW");
```

Use scalar filters and vector ranking together when the application needs metadata-aware search.

```csharp
QueryResult filtered = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
WHERE Label LIKE 'warm%'
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 10;
""")[0];
```

---

# Supported SQL

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/supported-sql
> Source file: manual/sql-language/supported-sql.md

DataVo SQL is a compact embedded-engine dialect. It is familiar if you know SQL, but it is not a PostgreSQL, SQLite, or SQL Server compatibility layer. This page documents the supported SQL syntax.

Start by creating and selecting a database.

```sql
CREATE DATABASE App;
USE App;
```

Create tables with primary keys, scalar columns, and vector columns.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Departments (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80)
);

CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  DepartmentId INT,
  Score FLOAT,
  IsActive BIT
);

CREATE TABLE ArchivedUsers (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  IsActive BIT
);

CREATE TABLE Embeddings (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Label VARCHAR(80),
  Emb VECTOR(3)
);
```

Insert rows with either a full-row form or a column-targeted form. Prefer the column-targeted form in application code because it is easier to read and safer to evolve.

```sql
INSERT INTO Users VALUES (1, 'Ada', 10, 98.5, true);

INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, DepartmentId, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (2, 'Grace', 10, 95.0, true);
```

Query rows with projection, filtering, ordering, and limits.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true AND Score > 90
ORDER BY Score DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Update and delete rows with predicates.

```sql
UPDATE Users
SET Score = 99.0
WHERE Id = 1;

DELETE FROM Users
WHERE Id = 2;
```

Create scalar indexes for lookup and ordering paths.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_users_name ON Users (Name);
CREATE INDEX ix_users_active_score ON Users (IsActive, Score);
```

Create vector indexes when the table stores embeddings.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_hnsw
ON Embeddings (Emb)
USING HNSW;

CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_flat
ON Embeddings (Emb)
USING FLAT;
```

Use joins when data is split across tables.

```sql
SELECT u.Name, d.Name AS Department
FROM Users u
INNER JOIN Departments d ON u.DepartmentId = d.Id;
```

Use grouped aggregates for summary queries.

```sql
SELECT IsActive, COUNT(*) AS UserCount, MAX(Score) AS HighestScore
FROM Users
GROUP BY IsActive
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;
```

Use `UNION` or `UNION ALL` when compatible SELECT branches should be combined.

```sql
SELECT Name FROM Users WHERE IsActive = true
UNION ALL
SELECT Name FROM ArchivedUsers WHERE IsActive = true;
```

Compact table storage after deletes with `VACUUM`.

```sql
VACUUM Users;
```

## SQL Support Summary

Supported: `CREATE DATABASE`/`USE`, `CREATE TABLE`/`DROP TABLE` (primary keys, defaults, scalar and vector columns), limited `ALTER TABLE ADD/DROP/MODIFY COLUMN`, scalar, vector and columnar indexes (`USING HNSW`, `USING FLAT`, `USING COLUMNAR`, with HNSW options in `WITH (...)`), core DML (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `VACUUM`), `SELECT`/`WHERE`/`ORDER BY`/`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`, aggregates with `GROUP BY`/`HAVING`, all major joins (`INNER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, `CROSS`), subqueries, non-recursive CTEs, `RANK() OVER (...)`, and `UNION`/`UNION ALL`. Other window functions, views, stored procedures, triggers, and PostgreSQL-dialect compatibility are **not** supported. See the [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility) for the authoritative feature status.

---

# CREATE TABLE

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/create-table
> Source file: manual/sql-language/create-table.md

`CREATE TABLE` defines the shape of rows DataVo can store. A table declaration gives each column a name and type, and it can mark a column as the primary key.

The most common table starts with an integer primary key.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  Score FLOAT,
  IsActive BIT
);
```

Insert a row immediately after creating the table to verify the shape.

```sql
INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (1, 'Ada', 98.5, true);

SELECT Id, Name, Score, IsActive
FROM Users
WHERE Id = 1;
```

Use `VARCHAR(n)` for text fields. The parser treats unrecognized string-like declarations as variable text, but explicit `VARCHAR(n)` keeps schemas readable.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Articles (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Title VARCHAR(200),
  Slug VARCHAR(200),
  Published BIT
);
```

Use `GUID`, `UUID`, or `UNIQUEIDENTIFIER` when application IDs are GUID-shaped.

```sql
CREATE TABLE ApiKeys (
  Id GUID PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(120),
  Revoked BIT
);
```

Use `VECTOR(n)` for embeddings. The dimension is part of the schema, so every value in that column must have the same length.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Documents (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Title VARCHAR(200),
  Embedding VECTOR(1536)
);
```

For 3D positions, `VEC3` and `FLOAT[3]` are both shorthand for `VECTOR(3)`. `VEC2`, `VEC4` and `FLOAT[n]`/`REAL[n]` work the same way.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Ships (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Position VEC3 NOT NULL,
  Velocity FLOAT[3]
);
```

Create scalar indexes after the table exists.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_users_name
ON Users (Name);

CREATE INDEX ix_users_active_score
ON Users (IsActive, Score);
```

A scalar index holds only rows whose indexed columns are all non-NULL: a row with a NULL key gets no entry, on every write path and when the index is built or rebuilt. `IS NULL` predicates therefore read rows, and any number of NULLs may share a `UNIQUE` column.

Create vector indexes on vector columns. Use `FLAT` for exact scan behavior on small datasets and `HNSW` when a larger dataset needs faster approximate nearest-neighbor search.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_documents_embedding_flat
ON Documents (Embedding)
USING FLAT;

CREATE INDEX idx_documents_embedding_hnsw
ON Documents (Embedding)
USING HNSW;
```

An HNSW index ranks by cosine distance unless you choose another metric. Positions need straight-line distance, so index them with `metric = 'euclidean'` (or `'l2'`). The metric is saved with the index and kept when the database is reopened. `WITH` also accepts the graph options `m`, `ef_construction`, `ef_search` and `enable_diversity_heuristic`; see [Vector Search and Indexes](/manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax) for their defaults and ranges.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_ships_position
ON Ships (Position)
USING HNSW WITH (metric = 'euclidean');
```

Create a columnar index on the numeric columns that analytical queries filter and aggregate on. It keeps a second copy of those columns as dense arrays, so a `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` or `MAX` that reads only indexed columns is computed many values at a time without reading rows.

```sql
CREATE INDEX cx_players
ON Players (Level, Gold, Ratio)
USING COLUMNAR;
```

- The columns must be `INT`, `BIGINT`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`, `BIT` or `DATE`. Any other type is rejected.
- It accelerates both `InMemory` and `Lsm` storage modes (legacy `Disk` mode accepts and records the index while queries read rows). On `Lsm`, the `COLUMNAR` spec is saved in the table directory and existing SSTables are backfilled once into format-v8 columnar segments; subsequent flushes and compactions write columnar chunks alongside rows, keeping only unflushed rows in memory.
- It is used for an aggregate without `GROUP BY` whose `WHERE` is an `AND` of comparisons between an indexed column and a literal, or `IS NULL` tests. Every column in the `WHERE` and in the aggregates must be in the index. Other queries, and queries inside a transaction, read rows.
- A comparison is left to the row scan when the index could not give exactly the same answer: a fractional literal against an `INT` column, a literal that is not exactly a `FLOAT`, a `BIT` or `DATE` column in the `WHERE`, or a floating-point column that holds a NaN (or floating-point `SUM` on multi-source LSM tables).
- It never serves a row lookup, so it does not replace a scalar index. Several columnar indexes on one table are kept as one. `DROP INDEX cx_players ON Players` removes it.
- On `InMemory`, it costs 4 or 8 bytes per row per column in RAM plus a write on insert/delete. On `Lsm`, flushed rows reside inside `.sst` columnar segments on disk rather than staying in the managed heap.

Schema changes are supported but limited. Adding a column rewrites existing rows and fills the new column with a default or null.

```sql
ALTER TABLE Users
ADD COLUMN CreatedBy VARCHAR(80) DEFAULT 'system';
```

Dropping or modifying columns is intentionally more restrictive when keys, foreign keys, or indexes are involved.

```sql
ALTER TABLE Users
DROP COLUMN CreatedBy;

ALTER TABLE Users
MODIFY COLUMN Name VARCHAR(160);
```

## DDL Support Summary

Supported DDL: `CREATE TABLE` (catalog metadata and table storage), integer primary keys, `VARCHAR(n)`, the scalar type set (`INT`, `BIGINT`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`, `BIT`, `DATE`, `GUID`), `VECTOR(n)` (with `VEC2`/`VEC3`/`VEC4` and `FLOAT[n]` shorthands), scalar and vector `CREATE INDEX` (`USING HNSW`, `USING FLAT`, `WITH (metric = 'cosine' | 'euclidean')`, and the HNSW graph options `m`, `ef_construction`, `ef_search` and `enable_diversity_heuristic`), columnar `CREATE INDEX ... USING COLUMNAR` (`InMemory` and persisted out-of-core `Lsm` storage; fixed-width numeric, `BIT` and `DATE` columns), `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` (rewrites rows and backfills null/default values), and limited `ALTER TABLE DROP/MODIFY COLUMN` (which rejects key, foreign-key, referenced, indexed, or incompatible changes). PostgreSQL domains and collations are **not** supported. See the [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility) for the authoritative feature status.

---

# Data Manipulation

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/data-manipulation
> Source file: manual/sql-language/data-manipulation.md

Data manipulation statements change table contents. The core workflow is straightforward: insert rows, update rows by predicate, delete rows by predicate, and vacuum storage after deletes when compaction matters.

Use column-targeted inserts for application code. The statement says exactly which columns receive values.

```sql
INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (1, 'Ada', 98.5, true);
```

Full-row inserts are shorter, but they depend on table column order.

```sql
INSERT INTO Users
VALUES (2, 'Grace', 95.0, true);
```

Insert vectors as bracketed numeric literals.

```sql
INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (1, 'red', '[1,0,0]');

INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (2, 'warm-red', '[0.9,0.1,0]');
```

Update rows with `SET` and `WHERE`.

```sql
UPDATE Users
SET Score = 99.0
WHERE Id = 1;
```

Update more than one column in the same statement.

```sql
UPDATE Users
SET Score = 100.0,
    IsActive = false
WHERE Name = 'Ada';
```

Delete rows with a predicate.

```sql
DELETE FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = false;
```

After many deletes, use `VACUUM` to compact the table.

```sql
VACUUM Users;
```

Wrap related writes in a transaction when they should commit or roll back together.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, Score, IsActive)
VALUES (3, 'Katherine', 97.0, true);

UPDATE Users
SET Score = 98.0
WHERE Id = 3;

COMMIT;
```

Rollback discards buffered changes in the current session.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

DELETE FROM Users
WHERE Id = 3;

ROLLBACK;
```

## DML Support Summary

Supported DML: column-targeted and full-row `INSERT` (the value count must match the columns), vector literal inserts (for example `'[1,0,0]'`), `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE ...` (with a fixed-width compiled fast path for narrow source-generated single-row shapes), `DELETE ... WHERE ...`, `VACUUM table`, and session-bound transactional DML (`BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`). `MERGE` and the PostgreSQL `COPY` protocol are **not** supported. See the [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility) for the authoritative feature status.

---

# Queries

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/queries
> Source file: manual/sql-language/queries.md

DataVo queries use familiar SQL clauses: choose columns, choose a table, filter rows, sort the result, and limit how much comes back.

The examples on this page use the following tables.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Departments (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80)
);

CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  DepartmentId INT,
  Score FLOAT,
  IsActive BIT
);

CREATE TABLE ArchivedUsers (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  IsActive BIT
);

CREATE TABLE Embeddings (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Label VARCHAR(80),
  Emb VECTOR(3)
);
```

The smallest useful query selects a few columns from a table.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name
FROM Users;
```

Use `WHERE` to filter rows.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
WHERE Score > 90;
```

Combine predicates when the application needs a narrower result set.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true AND Score BETWEEN 90 AND 100;
```

Use `LIKE` for simple string matching.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name
FROM Users
WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';
```

Use `IN` when a column can match one of several values.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name
FROM Users
WHERE Id IN (1, 3, 5);
```

Sort and page results with `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, and `OFFSET`.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name, Score
FROM Users
ORDER BY Score DESC, Id ASC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0;
```

Aggregate rows with `COUNT`, `SUM`, `MIN`, and `MAX`.

```sql
SELECT IsActive, COUNT(*) AS UserCount, MAX(Score) AS HighestScore
FROM Users
GROUP BY IsActive
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;
```

`COUNT` returns a 64-bit integer (`long`) on every query shape. `HAVING` may use aggregates the select list does not return, such as `HAVING COUNT(Tag) >= 2` with only `COUNT(*)` selected; each is computed on its own.

`HAVING` also works without `GROUP BY`. The whole filtered table is then one group, and `HAVING` decides whether its single result row is returned.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ActiveCount, AVG(Score) AS AverageScore
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;
```

Join tables when a query needs fields from both sides.

```sql
SELECT u.Name, d.Name AS Department
FROM Users u
INNER JOIN Departments d ON u.DepartmentId = d.Id;
```

Use `LEFT JOIN` when unmatched left rows should remain in the result.

```sql
SELECT u.Name, d.Name AS Department
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Departments d ON u.DepartmentId = d.Id;
```

Use subqueries for membership checks.

```sql
SELECT Id, Name
FROM Users
WHERE DepartmentId IN (
  SELECT Id
  FROM Departments
  WHERE Name LIKE 'Eng%'
);
```

Name an intermediate result with a common table expression. DataVo materializes it before running the main query; recursive CTEs are available to reactive queries only.

```sql
WITH HighScorers AS (
  SELECT Id, Name, DepartmentId FROM Users WHERE Score >= 90
)
SELECT d.Name, COUNT(*) AS N
FROM HighScorers h
INNER JOIN Departments d ON h.DepartmentId = d.Id
GROUP BY d.Name;
```

Rank rows within a partition with `RANK()`, the one supported window function.

```sql
SELECT Name, DepartmentId, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DepartmentId ORDER BY Score DESC) AS ScoreRank
FROM Users;
```

Combine compatible result sets with `UNION ALL`.

```sql
SELECT Name FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true
UNION ALL
SELECT Name FROM ArchivedUsers
WHERE IsActive = true;
```

Rank vectors with distance expressions. Lower distances sort first.

```sql
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 5;
```

## Streaming and Reactive Execution

- **Lazy `yield` row streaming:** Pass a single-table `SELECT` to `db.StreamQuery(sql, ...)` to read 1,024-row pages incrementally (`IEnumerable<DataVoRow>`) and stop early on `LIMIT` or `break` without buffering the whole result. See [Streaming Queries](/manual/client-interfaces/streaming-queries).
- **Standing incremental views:** Pass a supported `SELECT` to `db.Subscribe(sql, onChanged)` or `db.SubscribeZeroAlloc(sql, onChanged)` to receive Z-set deltas (`Added`, `Removed`, `Updated`) on `DispatchPendingNotifications()` instead of re-running queries. See [Live Reactive Views (Z-set IVM)](/manual/client-interfaces/reactive-views).

## Query Support Summary

Supported: projection and aliases; `WHERE` with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, comparisons, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE`, `IS [NOT] NULL` and vector-distance predicates; `ORDER BY` (including vector ranking), `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`; `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, with `DISTINCT` inside the parentheses; `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, including `HAVING` without `GROUP BY`; `INNER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL` and `CROSS` joins; `IN` and `EXISTS` subqueries; non-recursive common table expressions; `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`; `UNION` and `UNION ALL`; and vector distance (`<=>` cosine, `<->` Euclidean).

All of these return correct results, but not all are equally fast. Single-table filters and aggregates, and `INNER`/`LEFT` joins on integer keys, run on DataVo's typed paths; `DISTINCT`, `RIGHT`/`FULL`/`CROSS` joins, joins on text or `GUID` keys, an `OR` across two joined tables, CTEs, window functions and queries inside an explicit transaction run on the general evaluator, which is much slower on large tables. See [Query Planner And Fast Paths](/manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths) and the [SQL compatibility matrix](/manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility).

---

# Vector Search and Indexes

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax
> Source file: manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax.md

DataVo stores embeddings in `VECTOR(n)` columns, where `n` is the fixed number of floating-point dimensions in the vector. Every row in that column must use the same dimension. If your model emits 1536-dimensional embeddings, declare `VECTOR(1536)`. If you are learning with small examples, `VECTOR(3)` is easier to read.

Start by creating a table with an integer primary key, a label, and a vector column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Embeddings (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Label VARCHAR(80),
  Emb VECTOR(3)
);
```

Insert vectors as bracketed numeric literals. The examples below use three dimensions so the values are easy to inspect by eye.

```sql
INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (1, 'red', '[1,0,0]');

INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (2, 'green', '[0,1,0]');

INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (3, 'blue', '[0,0,1]');

INSERT INTO Embeddings (Id, Label, Emb)
VALUES (4, 'warm-red', '[0.9,0.1,0]');
```

To search vectors efficiently, create a vector index on the vector column. DataVo has two vector index families: `HNSW` and `FLAT`.

Use `FLAT` when you want perfect accuracy and the dataset is small enough that scanning every vector is acceptable. A flat index is simple: compare the query vector with every stored vector and return the exact nearest rows. It is a good default for tests, small local datasets, and correctness checks.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_flat
ON Embeddings (Emb)
USING FLAT;
```

Use `HNSW` when the dataset is large and query speed matters more than exact exhaustive search. HNSW builds an approximate nearest-neighbor graph so DataVo can avoid comparing against every vector. Use it only after measuring recall, build time, and query latency on your workload.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_hnsw
ON Embeddings (Emb)
USING HNSW;
```

`WITH (...)` sets the metric and the graph parameters. Every option is optional; an option you leave out keeps its default. Option names ignore case and underscores (`ef_construction` and `EfConstruction` are the same option).

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_tuned
ON Embeddings (Emb)
USING HNSW WITH (metric = 'cosine', m = 24, ef_construction = 128, ef_search = 96, enable_diversity_heuristic = true);
```

| Option | Default | Range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `metric` | `cosine` | `cosine`, `euclidean` (or `l2`) | The distance the index ranks by. Also accepted by `FLAT`. |
| `m` | `16` | 2 to 128 | Links each vector keeps per graph layer (twice as many on the bottom layer). More links raise recall, memory, and build time. |
| `ef_construction` | `64` | 1 to 4096 | Candidates examined when a vector is inserted. Higher values build a better graph more slowly. |
| `ef_search` | `64` | 1 to 4096 | The smallest candidate list of a search. Higher values raise recall and latency. |
| `enable_diversity_heuristic` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Prefers neighbors that are not close to one another, which keeps links between clusters. Leave it on for clustered data such as text embeddings; turning it off builds faster and can lose recall across clusters. |

The options are saved in the catalog with the index. When the graph has to be rebuilt from the table's rows, for example after its saved copy is lost, it is rebuilt with the same options. A value outside its range, an unknown option, or a graph option on a `FLAT` or B-tree index is an error and creates no index.

Once the data and index exist, write vector queries with distance operators. DataVo ranks nearer rows by smaller distance values, so nearest-neighbor queries normally sort ascending and use `LIMIT`.

Cosine distance uses the `<=>` operator. It is commonly used for text embeddings because it compares direction more than magnitude.

```sql
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 3;
```

L2 distance uses the `<->` operator. It measures Euclidean distance, which is useful when absolute geometric distance matters for your embedding space.

```sql
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <-> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 3;
```

You can combine vector ranking with ordinary scalar filters. This is the common shape for application search: restrict the candidate set by metadata, then rank the remaining rows by vector distance.

```sql
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
WHERE Label LIKE 'warm%'
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 10;
```

## Filtered searches

A filtered search still returns the exact number of rows the `LIMIT` asks for when that many rows pass the filter. DataVo asks the index for more candidates than the `LIMIT` (about `LIMIT / selectivity`), tests the filter on each candidate's stored row, and builds only the rows that pass. Two cost rules keep selective filters fast:

- When the filter needs so many candidates that walking the HNSW graph would cost more than comparing every stored vector, the HNSW index scans its vectors instead. A graph search widens its beam with the number of candidates requested (roughly `log2(n) × k × 1.5`), and each beam slot costs a fixed amount of queue work and cache misses plus about 2.4 distance computations; an exact scan costs one distance computation per vector. The index compares the two estimates per query. With the measured constants the scan wins once the beam exceeds about 9% of the vectors at 384 dimensions and 20% at 1,536. The scan is exact, so this routing can only raise recall. In C#, `HNSWIndex.EnableExactScanCostRouting = false` turns it off.
- When even the widest candidate search finds too few passing rows (by default the candidate count is doubled at most twice), DataVo finds the passing rows first with a table scan and ranks only those by the index's stored vectors. That answer is exact as well. Before v0.4 such a query returned fewer rows than its `LIMIT` even though more rows matched.

The same applies to a filtered search over a join, such as `FROM Docs d JOIN Authors a ON d.AuthorId = a.Id WHERE a.Country = 'DE'`: the candidates are joined and filtered in stored form, and a joined table is read by primary key only for the candidates that refer to it.

You can also use a vector distance predicate directly in `WHERE`. This returns only rows closer than the threshold and then orders the survivors by the same distance expression.

```sql
SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
WHERE Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' < 0.25
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 10;
```

## Large embeddings

For production-sized embeddings, the same SQL shape works with larger dimensions. The only difference is the column declaration and the vector literal length.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Documents (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Title VARCHAR(200),
  ContentEmbedding VECTOR(1536)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_documents_embedding
ON Documents (ContentEmbedding)
USING HNSW;
```

Pick `FLAT` first when you are validating correctness. Move to `HNSW` when the table grows large enough that exact scans are too slow for your latency target.

---

# SQL Compatibility Matrix

> Source route: /manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility
> Source file: manual/sql-language/sql-compatibility.md

DataVo SQL is its own dialect, smaller than PostgreSQL, SQLite or SQL Server. This page states which constructs it accepts, and, because performance depends on it, which of them run on a typed execution path and which on the general evaluator.

The distinction matters. Every construct listed as supported returns the correct result on both active storage engines. But a query that a typed path accepts reads cells directly from stored rows and allocates little, while a query on the general path builds a dictionary for every row it reads, which costs kilobytes per row and can make a million-row query take seconds instead of milliseconds. [Query Planner And Fast Paths](/manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths) explains the typed paths.

The core lifecycle:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE App;
USE App;

CREATE TABLE Departments (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80));
CREATE TABLE Users (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80), DepartmentId INT, IsActive BIT);

INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, DepartmentId, IsActive) VALUES (1, 'Ada', 10, true);
UPDATE Users SET IsActive = false WHERE Id = 1;
DELETE FROM Users WHERE Id = 1;
```

Joins, grouping and filters, including `HAVING` on an aggregate without `GROUP BY`:

```sql
SELECT d.Name AS Department, COUNT(*) AS UserCount
FROM Users u
INNER JOIN Departments d ON u.DepartmentId = d.Id
WHERE u.IsActive = true OR u.Name LIKE 'A%'
GROUP BY d.Name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users WHERE IsActive = true HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
```

Vector search is ordinary SQL:

```sql
CREATE TABLE Embeddings (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Label VARCHAR(80), Emb VECTOR(3));
CREATE INDEX idx_embeddings_hnsw ON Embeddings (Emb) USING HNSW WITH (m = 16, ef_search = 64);

SELECT Id, Label, Emb <=> '[1,0,0]' AS distance
FROM Embeddings
WHERE Label LIKE 'warm%'
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 5;
```

## Statements and clauses

| Feature | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CREATE DATABASE`, `USE`, `DROP` | Supported | |
| `CREATE TABLE`, `DROP TABLE` | Supported | Primary keys, defaults, scalar and vector columns. See [CREATE TABLE](/manual/sql-language/create-table). |
| `ALTER TABLE` | Limited | `ADD COLUMN`; `DROP`/`MODIFY COLUMN` reject key, indexed, referenced or incompatible changes. |
| `CREATE INDEX` | Supported | B-tree (single and composite), `USING HNSW`, `USING FLAT`, `USING COLUMNAR`; `WITH (metric, m, ef_construction, ef_search, enable_diversity_heuristic)` for vector indexes. |
