| `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `VACUUM` | Supported | See [Data Manipulation](/manual/sql-language/data-manipulation). |
| Transactions | Supported | `BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`; snapshot isolation, not serializable. |
| `SELECT` projection, aliases, `DISTINCT` | Supported | `SELECT DISTINCT` runs on the general path. |
| `WHERE` with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, comparisons, `IS [NOT] NULL`, `LIKE`, `NOT LIKE` | Supported | Typed path on one table and within one table of a join. |
| `IN (list)`, `BETWEEN` | Supported | A `BETWEEN` on a clustered primary key is a key-range seek. |
| `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, `OFFSET` | Supported | `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` keeps a bounded top-k on the typed scan and typed join. |
| Aggregates `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` | Supported | Including `DISTINCT` inside the parentheses (general path). `COUNT(DISTINCT *)` is a parse error. |
| `GROUP BY`, `HAVING` | Supported | `HAVING` without `GROUP BY` applies to the single group (v0.4). |
| `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN` | Supported | Typed hash join on integer equality keys, any number of tables. |
| `RIGHT JOIN`, `FULL OUTER JOIN`, `CROSS JOIN` | Supported | General path. |
| Joins on text or `GUID` keys, `OR` across two joined tables, self-joins | Supported | General path. |
| Subqueries | Supported | `IN (SELECT ...)`, `EXISTS`, `NOT EXISTS`. |
| Common table expressions | Supported | Non-recursive `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)`, materialized before the main query. `WITH RECURSIVE` is available to reactive queries only. |
| `UNION`, `UNION ALL` | Supported | |
| `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` | Not supported | |
| Window functions | Limited | `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` only. No `ROW_NUMBER`, frames, or other window functions. |
| Scalar functions | Limited | `UPPER` and `LOWER`. No `LEN`, `CASE`, `CAST`, `COALESCE` or date functions. |
| Vector distance | Supported | `<=>` (cosine), `<->` (Euclidean) in projections, `WHERE` and `ORDER BY`. |
| Views (`CREATE VIEW`) | Not supported | [Live Reactive Views (Z-set IVM)](/manual/client-interfaces/reactive-views) (`Subscribe` / `SubscribeZeroAlloc`) cover continuous queries from C#. |
| Stored procedures, triggers, user-defined functions | Not supported | |
| PostgreSQL system catalogs (`pg_class`, ...) | Not supported | |
| Security commands | Supported | `CREATE USER`, `CREATE ROLE`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `LOGIN`, `LOGOUT`, `SHOW USERS/ROLES/GRANTS`. Not a PostgreSQL role system. |

## Types

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `INT`, `BIGINT` | 32- and 64-bit integers. A single `INT` primary key is clustered on LSM. |
| `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE` | `FLOAT` is **32-bit** in DataVo (SQLite's `REAL` and SQL Server's `FLOAT` are 64-bit); use `DOUBLE` for 64-bit values. |
| `BIT` | Boolean. Write values and comparisons as `TRUE`/`FALSE` (any case); `1`/`0` and `'true'`/`'false'` are also read as booleans. |
| `DATE` | Materializes as `DataVoDate`. |
| `VARCHAR(n)` | Stored as UTF-8. Comparisons and ordering are ordinal (by character code), not collation-aware or case-insensitive. |
| `GUID` (`UUID`, `UNIQUEIDENTIFIER`) | A single `GUID` primary key is clustered on LSM. |
| `VECTOR(n)` (`VEC2`, `VEC3`, `VEC4`, `FLOAT[n]`) | Fixed dimension per column, 32-bit floats. `VECTOR` is a keyword, so a column cannot be named `Vector`. |

---

# Storage Modes

> Source route: /manual/storage-engine/storage-modes
> Source file: manual/storage-engine/storage-modes.md

`StorageMode` chooses where DataVo stores rows. Pick the simplest mode that matches the job: in-memory for tests, disk for straightforward persistence, and LSM for high-throughput persisted workloads.

Use in-memory mode for examples and unit tests.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});
```

Use disk mode when you want simple file-backed storage and WAL configuration.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Disk,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_data",
    WalEnabled = true
});
```

Use LSM mode for persisted write-heavy experiments. Strict fsync is the default durability setting to start with.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

Relaxed LSM is the benchmark/cache mode. It can be much faster because it does not wait for synchronous stable-storage flush on each acknowledged write.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_cache",
    LsmStrictFsync = false
});
```

## Storage Mode Support Summary

`StorageMode.InMemory` (ephemeral, with zero-alloc PK point lookups for tests, caching, and low-latency workloads), `StorageMode.Lsm` (WAL-covered MemTables, SSTables, manifests, clustered PKs, and compaction), and `StorageMode.Disk` (file-backed local tables with WAL options; **legacy**, see below) are the embedded storage modes. `StorageMode.Wasm` (`DataVo.Browser`) is an `Experimental / Playground Lane` mode for the interactive documentation site only (not production-ready and not published on npm), and `StorageMode.Custom` provides custom storage injection.

`StorageMode.Lsm` is the durable mode DataVo is heading toward production with. `StorageMode.Disk` is a legacy mode: it stays available, but it receives no further durability work, and it is not crash-safe for `UPDATE` (see [WAL And Durability](./wal-and-durability.md#known-limitations)). New applications should use Lsm.

Disk and Lsm directories are served by one engine per process: contexts and connections opened on the same directory share it, and a `datavo.lock` file keeps other processes out while it is open. See [LSM Mode](./lsm-mode.md#opening-the-same-directory-twice).

---

# LSM Mode

> Source route: /manual/storage-engine/lsm-mode
> Source file: manual/storage-engine/lsm-mode.md

`StorageMode.Lsm` is DataVo's high-throughput persisted backend. It is the mode behind the headline write-path benchmark results.

Start with strict durability.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

Writes first go to the data directory's commit log (`commit.wal`, one record per statement or transaction) and then to each table's active MemTable. The active MemTable is designed around arena-backed storage so steady-state write allocation stays low.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Events (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  Value INT
);

INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name, Value)
VALUES (1, 'started', 100);
```

When the active MemTable crosses 32 MB, DataVo freezes that generation, swaps in a new MemTable, and lets a background worker flush the frozen generation to SSTables.

```text
write
  -> append commit-log record (one per statement or transaction)
  -> active MemTable
  -> freeze at 32 MB
  -> background SSTable flush
  -> manifest edit
  -> commit-log records covered by every table's SSTables are pruned
```

Relaxed LSM mode uses the same broad storage shape, but it does not wait for synchronous WAL fsync before acknowledging writes.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_relaxed",
    LsmStrictFsync = false
});
```

## What SSTables Do

An SSTable (Sorted String Table, `.sst`) is an immutable, page-aligned file produced when a 32 MB MemTable flushes or when background compaction merges older files:

- **Fast Primary-Key Point Lookups:** Entries are stored sorted by clustered `RowKey` inside 4 KiB page-aligned data blocks with a sparse block index and a per-file blocked Bloom filter. Point lookups avoid absent files in memory and read at most one block on a hit (`~223–236 ns` on 100K rows).
- **Predictable Sequential I/O & Crash Safety:** Because SSTables are never modified in place, writes go sequentially to a temp file, `fsync` before atomic rename, and become visible in one manifest version edit alongside commit-log pruning.
- **Out-of-Core Columnar Segments (v8 format):** On tables with a `[Columnar]` index (`CREATE INDEX ... USING COLUMNAR`), flush and compaction also write 4,096-row aligned columnar chunks, NULL/NaN masks, deleted-key (tombstone) runs, and per-chunk min/max zone maps directly inside each `.sst` file, without touching row blocks or point-lookup speed.

## Reopening a Database

An LSM directory keeps its schema (`Catalog.xml`), its data (SSTables plus the commit log), any active `COLUMNAR` index spec, and its transaction-id high-water mark. Opening a new context on the same directory restores all of it.

```csharp
using (var db = new DataVoContext(config))
{
    db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App");
    db.Execute("USE App");
    db.Execute("CREATE TABLE Events (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80))");
    db.Execute("INSERT INTO Events (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'started')");
}

using var reopened = new DataVoContext(config);
reopened.Execute("USE App");
reopened.Execute("SELECT * FROM Events WHERE Id = 1"); // returns the row
```

What happens to each kind of index on open:

- **Primary-key and secondary B-tree indexes** are stored as their own key spaces ("index tables") of `(key, row id)` entries in keyed SSTables under the table's `.idx` directory. An index change is staged in the same write unit as the row change, so it reaches the commit log in the same record, and rows and indexes recover together after a crash. Opening a database does not rebuild them. A clustered table's primary key is not stored at all: the rows are keyed by it.
- **HNSW graphs** are written to a snapshot file on a clean close, stamped with the commit-log sequence number they reflect. On open, the snapshot is loaded and only rows written after that number are inserted into or removed from the graph; if more than half the rows changed, or the snapshot is missing or fails its checksum, the graph is rebuilt from the rows. After a crash the graph is therefore rebuilt or caught up, never trusted beyond what the rows say.
- **FLAT vector indexes** are rebuilt from the rows on open. They hold only the vectors, so the rebuild is a sequential read.
- **Columnar indexes (`[Columnar]` / `USING COLUMNAR`)** live inside the SSTables themselves (format version 8). Only the unflushed tail stays in memory, so nothing is rebuilt: covered filters and aggregates stream 4,096-row chunks from the memory-mapped `.sst` segments and skip chunks whose min/max zone maps rule out the predicate. Opening a database and answering a first `SUM` over 1,000,000 flushed rows took 13.7 ms with the files in the OS page cache.

## Opening the Same Directory Twice

Contexts and ADO.NET connections in one process that open the same directory share a single engine. The engine stays open until the last of them is disposed. They must use equivalent configuration, otherwise the second open throws `DatabaseInUseException` naming the setting that differs.

A directory can be open in only one process at a time. DataVo holds a `datavo.lock` file while the engine is open, and a second process gets `DatabaseInUseException`.

## LSM Support Summary

The LSM engine provides an arena-backed MemTable, clustered `INT` and `GUID` primary keys, a single commit log per data directory (records are pruned once every table has flushed them; directories written by earlier versions with per-table WAL files are migrated automatically on first open), a 32 MB MemTable flush threshold (an internal constant, not a public tuning knob), a background flush pipeline that runs outside the foreground write path, background SSTable compaction, memory-mapped SSTable reads (`LsmReadMode.Auto`; `PositionalRead` uses file reads instead), secondary indexes persisted as index tables in the same commit as their rows, HNSW graph snapshots caught up from the commit log on open, and persistent format-v8 columnar SSTable segments with per-chunk zone-map pruning. The on-disk format does not yet carry a long-term cross-version compatibility guarantee prior to 1.0.

---

# WAL And Durability

> Source route: /manual/storage-engine/wal-and-durability
> Source file: manual/storage-engine/wal-and-durability.md

Durability settings decide when DataVo is allowed to acknowledge a write. The fastest setting is not always the safest setting, so benchmark numbers should always be read with the durability mode attached.

Disk mode can use WAL with normal buffered writes.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Disk,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_data",
    WalEnabled = true,
    SyncDiskWrites = false
});
```

Turn on synchronous disk writes when the workload needs a stronger flush setting.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Disk,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_data",
    WalEnabled = true,
    SyncDiskWrites = true
});
```

LSM strict mode waits for WAL durability before acknowledging writes. This is the conservative production-style setting.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_strict",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

LSM relaxed mode acknowledges after the OS-buffered WAL append path. It is appropriate for caches, rebuildable data, and benchmark ceilings, but recent acknowledged writes can be lost on power or kernel failure.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_relaxed",
    LsmStrictFsync = false
});
```

When documenting or comparing results, include the storage mode and durability setting next to the number.

```text
Good:
  DataVo LSM Relaxed, 1-thread throughput: 1,333,227 ops/s

Misleading:
  DataVo throughput: 1,333,227 ops/s
```

## Durability Support Summary

Supported: disk WAL (`WalEnabled`, on by default for disk mode), disk sync writes (`SyncDiskWrites = true`), LSM strict fsync (`LsmStrictFsync = true`, which waits for WAL durability before acknowledging writes), LSM relaxed OS-buffered mode (faster, but can lose recent writes on power or kernel failure), and WAL checkpoint settings. Relaxed throughput must **not** be presented as strict durability.

## Crash Atomicity in Lsm Mode

Every SQL statement, and every explicit transaction at `COMMIT`, is written to the data directory's commit log (`commit.wal`) as **one** checksummed record. After a crash, recovery applies each record completely or not at all, so a multi-row `UPDATE` or a transaction that touches several tables is never half-applied. In strict mode a statement returns only after its record is durable; concurrent statements share fsyncs.

## Visibility and Failed Statements in Lsm Mode

A statement's changes (rows, index entries, and change notifications) become visible to other sessions only after its commit record is durable, and statements publish in commit order. Write locks are held until then, so a concurrent statement on the same table never checks its keys against unpublished changes. A statement that fails is discarded entirely: it writes no commit record and leaves no visible change.

## Known Limitations

- **Disk mode is legacy** and not crash-safe for `UPDATE`: it writes the new row version and removes the old one as two separate durable steps, so a crash between them can lose the row. Use Lsm for new applications.
- **In-memory and Disk transactions.** `COMMIT` re-checks primary keys and UNIQUE values for every table before applying anything. A foreign-key conflict found while applying a later table leaves the earlier tables of that `COMMIT` applied in these modes; Lsm discards the whole transaction.

---

# Transactions and MVCC

> Source route: /manual/storage-engine/transactions-acid-mvcc
> Source file: manual/storage-engine/transactions-acid-mvcc.md

DataVo's concurrency model is designed for embedded workloads where many reads should stay cheap while writes remain coordinated enough to keep table and index state consistent. In plain terms: point reads are optimized so they do not have to serialize through a global lock, while writes use row and table coordination where the engine needs a clear mutation boundary.

The simplest transaction is an explicit group of statements followed by `COMMIT`. DataVo buffers the transaction's changes in the session and applies them when the transaction commits.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, IsActive)
VALUES (1, 'Ada', true);

UPDATE Users
SET IsActive = false
WHERE Id = 1;

COMMIT;
```

If the transaction should not be applied, use `ROLLBACK`. The buffered changes are discarded.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, IsActive)
VALUES (2, 'Grace', true);

ROLLBACK;
```

Transactions are session-bound. If your application uses explicit sessions with `DataVoContext.Execute(sql, sessionId)`, the transaction belongs to that session. This lets one part of an embedded application hold a transaction open without accidentally mixing it with statements from another logical workflow.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});

Guid sessionId = Guid.NewGuid();

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App", sessionId);
db.Execute("USE App", sessionId);
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE Users (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(80))", sessionId);

db.Execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION", sessionId);
db.Execute("INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name) VALUES (1, 'Ada')", sessionId);
db.Execute("COMMIT", sessionId);
```

MVCC, or multi-version concurrency control, is the part of the engine that lets reads reason about row visibility without forcing every read to block every writer. Each explicit transaction reads from a **snapshot** taken at `BEGIN`.

## Snapshot isolation

A snapshot is ordered by commit, not by transaction start. It contains exactly the commits that had *finished* when the transaction began:

- A transaction never sees a commit that finished after it began — including the commit of a transaction that began *earlier* and was still open (or committing) at its `BEGIN`.
- Auto-commit statements follow the same rule: a statement that was still running when a transaction began is invisible to it, even if it finishes a moment later.
- Rows changed or deleted after the snapshot was taken are read as they were (the engine keeps the old row images while any snapshot may need them).

```sql
-- Session A                         -- Session B
BEGIN;                               BEGIN;
UPDATE Accounts SET Bal = 90
WHERE Id = 1;
COMMIT;
                                     -- Still reads Bal = 100: A committed after B began.
                                     SELECT Bal FROM Accounts WHERE Id = 1;
                                     COMMIT;
```

`BEGIN` waits for write statements and commits that are already in flight to finish publishing, so a snapshot never contains half of one. The wait is bounded by `LockAcquireTimeoutMs`.

## Reading your own writes

Every statement inside a transaction — `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, joins, subqueries, index lookups, and compiled LINQ `ExecuteUpdate`/`ExecuteDelete`, which run as SQL — reads through the snapshot *plus the transaction's own uncommitted writes*. Statements build on each other exactly as in standard SQL:

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, IsActive) VALUES (3, 'Linus', true);
UPDATE Users SET Name = 'Linus T.' WHERE Name = 'Linus';   -- matches the buffered insert
UPDATE Users SET IsActive = false WHERE Name = 'Linus T.'; -- matches the updated value
DELETE FROM Users WHERE IsActive = false AND Id = 3;       -- removes it again
COMMIT;                                                     -- nothing is written for Id 3
```

Repeated updates of one row coalesce into a single pending version. Key checks inside the transaction account for its own writes: a key it deleted is free again, a key it inserted is taken.

`SAVEPOINT name`, `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` and `RELEASE SAVEPOINT name` restore the transaction's buffered inserts, updates and deletes to the state at the savepoint; savepoints created after it are discarded.

## Write conflicts

Two transactions that change the same row conflict, and the first to commit wins. The second one fails with a conflict error — either at the `UPDATE`/`DELETE` statement, if the other commit already finished, or at its own `COMMIT`. A failed `COMMIT` ends the transaction; retry it from `BEGIN`.

At `COMMIT` the engine also re-checks, against what other sessions committed meanwhile, the primary and unique keys of buffered inserts and of updated values, and the foreign keys of buffered inserts and of updated rows (an update cannot point a child at a parent that was deleted in the meantime). Swapping or rotating key values among the transaction's own rows is allowed: the commit removes every old row before it writes any new one.

## Atomic commit

A `COMMIT` is all or nothing. Write conflicts and key checks run before anything is applied. The foreign keys of buffered inserts are checked after the commit's deletes and updates are applied (a child may reference a parent the same transaction inserts), so a later failure must undo earlier steps: on LSM the whole commit is one write batch, discarded on failure; the in-memory engine journals every applied change and undoes it. A failed `COMMIT` leaves rows, indexes and version metadata exactly as they were.

## Concurrency behaviour

Readers outside transactions never wait for MVCC. While at least one transaction is open, a statement that reads through a snapshot and a write statement that must record versions for it do not overlap: each waits for the other's *statement* to finish (never for a whole transaction), at most `LockAcquireTimeoutMs`, after which the waiting statement fails with a timeout error and the transaction stays usable. Write statements do not wait for each other because of MVCC; they coordinate only through row and table locks.

Version metadata and retained row images are dropped as soon as no open snapshot can need them. The cleanup work follows the commits made while transactions were open; it never scans the whole table or version map.

## Isolation contract

The isolation level is **snapshot isolation**. It prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, lost updates and read skew, and a transaction's repeated reads (including with predicates) return the same rows. It is not serializable: **write skew** is possible — two transactions that each read rows the other updates, and update disjoint rows, can both commit.

```sql
-- Both see two doctors on call; each takes a different one off call; both commit.
-- Session A                                   -- Session B
BEGIN;                                         BEGIN;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM OnCall WHERE Active = true;
                                               SELECT COUNT(*) FROM OnCall WHERE Active = true;
UPDATE OnCall SET Active = false WHERE Id = 1;
                                               UPDATE OnCall SET Active = false WHERE Id = 2;
COMMIT;                                        COMMIT;   -- succeeds: no row was written by both
```

Guard such invariants with a row both transactions update (for example a counter row), which turns the skew into a write conflict.

Durability depends on the storage configuration. For the LSM engine, use `LsmStrictFsync = true` when committed writes must wait for the WAL to reach stable storage.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});
```

Relaxed LSM mode is useful for benchmarks and rebuildable data, but it has a different contract: recent acknowledged writes can be lost on power or kernel failure because the WAL is not synchronously forced to stable storage.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_cache",
    LsmStrictFsync = false
});
```

## ACID & Isolation Contract

Supported: session-bound `BEGIN TRANSACTION`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK` and savepoints (DML is buffered until commit or rollback); snapshot isolation ordered by commit; read-your-own-writes across chained DML; first-committer-wins write conflicts; atomic `COMMIT` on every storage engine; single-row lock-free reads; per-table write locks and row-level write coordination for auto-commit statements; strict LSM commit durability (`LsmStrictFsync = true`); and disk sync writes (`SyncDiskWrites = true`). DataVo does **not** guarantee serializability (write skew is possible) or full ACID equivalence to PostgreSQL or SQLite.

---

# Query Planner And Fast Paths

> Source route: /manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths
> Source file: manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths.md

DataVo does not have a general cost-based optimizer. It has one general evaluator that can run every supported query, and a set of **typed paths**, each of which recognises a family of query shapes and runs them directly against stored rows. A `SELECT` is offered to the typed paths first. A typed path either produces exactly the rows the general evaluator would, in the same order, or declines; declining is never an error. This page describes what each path accepts and how it works, because whether a query lands on a typed path is the main factor in its speed.

## Why the distinction matters

The general evaluator materializes every row it reads as a dictionary from column name to boxed value, then evaluates `WHERE`, joins, grouping and projection over those dictionaries. That is flexible and slow: 2–4 KB of allocation per row read, so a million-row scan allocates gigabytes and takes seconds. The typed paths decode only the columns a query names, keep values unboxed, and build a result row only for rows that are returned. On the 1,000,000-row benchmark, moving `OR`, `LIKE` and multi-table joins onto typed paths took those queries from 1.7–5.0 s to 20–100 ms ([DataVo vs SQLite](/manual/performance/datavo-vs-sqlite)).

## The order in which paths are tried

```text
SELECT
  -> typed single-table path       (one table, no join)
       index point lookup | primary-key range seek | columnar aggregate | full typed scan
  -> typed join path               (INNER/LEFT joins on integer keys)
       hash join | index-driven probe | key-only bit set
  -> general path
       vector predicate path | nearest-neighbour path | general evaluator
```

Both typed paths decline inside an explicit transaction (they do not read through the transaction's MVCC snapshot), and for `SELECT DISTINCT`, common table expressions, computed expressions in the select list, and window functions. Those queries run on the general path, as do `RIGHT`/`FULL`/`CROSS` joins, joins on text or `GUID` keys, and an `OR` that spans two joined tables.

## Typed single-table path

Accepts one table whose `WHERE` is built from `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, comparisons between a column and a literal or bound parameter (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`), `IS [NOT] NULL`, `LIKE` and `NOT LIKE`, with any mix of aggregates, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`. It picks the cheapest access method:

- **Index point lookup.** An equality on the primary key or on a column with a single-column B-tree index reads the matching row keys in one index lookup and then reads those rows by key.
- **Primary-key range seek.** On a clustered LSM table, a range on the key (`BETWEEN`, or `>=` with `<`) becomes a seek into the SSTables and a sequential read of the range. On the InMemory engine, the integer key map answers ranges from a sorted copy of its keys, built by the first range query (8 bytes per key) and kept current by logging later inserts; a range covering more than a quarter of the table is scanned instead.
- **Columnar aggregate.** A `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` or `MAX` without `GROUP BY`, whose filter compares numeric columns of a columnar index with values (`AND` and `OR`, `IS [NOT] NULL`), is answered from the index's column buffers with SIMD kernels. On LSM the flushed part comes from columnar SSTable segments, and a chunk whose zone map (min, max, NULL and NaN flags) rules out the predicate is skipped without being read.
- **Full typed scan.** Otherwise every row is visited in storage order, the filtered columns are decoded, and the predicate is evaluated.

Details that matter for correctness and cost:

- **Three-valued logic.** The parser pushes `NOT` down into the comparisons, and `WHERE` keeps only rows that evaluate to true, so treating any comparison with a NULL as false gives SQL's result for `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`.
- **Text on stored bytes.** On the LSM engine rows are serialized, and decoding a .NET string per row per text column used to cost 36–46 MB per million-row query. Now the row walk records where each filtered text value lies, and `=`, `<>`, `LIKE`, `NOT LIKE` and `IS [NOT] NULL` read the UTF-8 bytes in place. Byte equality is ordinal string equality for valid UTF-8, and a `LIKE` pattern's literal runs can only match whole characters, so the answer is the same. The one case bytes cannot decide is `_` against non-ASCII text, because `_` matches one UTF-16 character; that value is decoded and matched as before. A text column the query also returns is decoded only for matching rows.
- **`LIKE` matching.** `SqlLikePattern` handles prefix (`'S0042%'`), suffix and substring (`'%042-%'`) patterns with span searches, and any other pattern with a wildcard matcher.
- **Grouping.** Aggregates go into a hash table keyed by the group value. A one-column key is looked up by its value without boxing, and each aggregate lives in an array indexed by group number. `HAVING`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` are applied to the groups before any group becomes a result row. An aggregate without `GROUP BY` uses its single group directly.
- **Top-k.** `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` without a usable index keeps the k best rows in a bounded list. A scanned row's sort keys are compared with the kept rows in place, and only a row that enters the list has its keys copied, so the scan allocates nothing per row.
- **Floating-point sums on LSM.** A columnar `SUM` or `AVG` of a `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE` column is left to the row scan whenever the index cannot read in key order, which is the case on LSM while an unflushed tail exists. Floating-point addition is not associative, and a different order can change the last bits of the result. The columnar path answers only when it can return exactly the row scan's bits. Integer sums, counts, minimums and maximums are always pushed.

## Typed join path

Accepts `INNER` and `LEFT` joins of any number of tables on integer equality keys, with per-table `WHERE` conditions (including `OR` and `LIKE` within one table), aggregates with or without `GROUP BY`, and joined rows, either all of them or a top-N with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`.

- **Hash join.** One table is streamed: the largest when every join is INNER, the `FROM` table when a `LEFT JOIN` must keep its rows or rows are returned without a top-N. Every other table is hashed on its join key, keeping only the columns read after the join (select list, grouping, aggregates, sort keys, conditions of a `LEFT`-joined table, and the next join key). Each streamed row is extended table by table; a `LEFT` step pads an unmatched row with NULLs.
- **Condition placement.** A condition on an INNER-joined table filters it while it is hashed. A condition on a `LEFT`-joined table is tested after the join, against the matched row or the NULL padding, which is what SQL means. (Applying it before the join was correctness bug `B1`.)
- **Key-only tables as bit sets.** A joined table that contributes nothing but its key, as in `LEFT JOIN Customers c ... WHERE c.Id IS NULL`, `COUNT(c.Id)`, or an existence-only inner join, needs only to answer "is this key present, and how many times?" Its keys are collected while the table is scanned. If they are distinct and span at most 64 values per key, they become a bit per value of their range (`DenseInt64Set`): 12.5 KB for 100,000 consecutive keys, where a hash table with counts took 2.9 MB, and a probe becomes a bit test. Repeated or scattered keys are hashed with their counts as before.
- **Index-driven probe.** When every join is INNER and a hashed table has few keys, the streamed table may be read through a single-column index on its join column instead of scanned. A sample of 32 keys estimates how many rows the index would name; the index is used when that is at most an eighth of the table. Rows are read in key order, the order a scan would visit them, so results are identical.

## General path

**Vector search.** `ORDER BY <vector column> <=> @q LIMIT k` (or `<->`), with or without a filter or a join, is planned here; see [Vector Search and Indexes](/manual/sql-language/vector-search-syntax#filtered-searches) for how filtered searches choose between the HNSW graph, an exact scan, and a filter-first scan. A distance threshold in `WHERE` (`Emb <=> @q < 0.25`) can use the index to prefilter candidates (`EnableVectorPredicateFastPath`).

**The general evaluator.** Everything else. Since v0.4 it runs a join once per query: `WHERE` is split into top-level `AND` conjuncts, conjuncts on one table filter it before the join only when that gives the same result, and the rest are tested on the joined rows. An optional Volcano-style operator pipeline (`EnableVolcanoExecution`, off by default) exists for planner experiments and spill-to-disk tests; leave it off.

## Compiled queries

Source-generated queries skip SQL parsing at run time. `[DataVoQuery]` methods compile a fixed SQL statement, and `DataVoTable<T>` lambdas (`Where`, `Count`, `Sum`, `Min`, `Max`, `Any`, `FirstOrDefault`, `SingleOrDefault`) are intercepted at build time and turned into code that reads cells from stored bytes. See [Roslyn Source Generators](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators).

```csharp
public static partial class PlayerQueries
{
    [DataVoQuery("SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Id = @id")]
    public static partial PlayerRow? GetPlayer(DataVoContext db, int id);

    // Narrow fixed-width single-row update: when the row is found through the integer
    // primary-key lane and can be patched safely, the stored bytes are patched in place.
    [DataVoQuery("UPDATE Players SET Level = @level WHERE Id = @id")]
    public static partial int UpdateLevel(DataVoContext db, int id, int level);
}
```

## SQL DATE row contract

SQL `DATE` columns materialize as `DataVo.Core.DataVoDate` in the row APIs. `CellValue.AsDate()` and compiled `GetDate`/`GetDateOrNull` return it; on modern .NET, `DataVoDate.FromDateOnly(...)`, `ToDateOnly()`, `CellValue.AsDateOnly()` and compiled `GetDateOnly`/`GetDateOnlyOrNull` convert explicitly. Persisted `DATE` bytes are unchanged.

## What the planner does not do

- It does not use a secondary index to drive a `GROUP BY`. SQLite reads an indexed key in order and groups without a hash table, which is why it is 2.3 times faster on a 125,000-group `GROUP BY` over an indexed column.
- It does not reorder joins by cost beyond choosing the streamed table and the index-driven probe described above.
- The typed paths keep no table statistics; the index-probe decision samples keys at run time.
- Typed paths do not run inside explicit transactions; reads in a transaction take the general path.

---

# Connecting to DataVo

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/datavo-context-api
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/datavo-context-api.md

DataVo is embedded in your .NET process. There is no server to start, no socket to open, and no connection pool to configure for the core API. You create a `DataVoContext`, choose a storage mode, and execute SQL directly against the engine.

The fastest way to prove the engine is working is to use in-memory storage. This keeps the example self-contained and avoids creating files while you learn the API.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.Contracts.Results;
using DataVo.Core.StorageEngine.Config;

using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App");
db.Execute("USE App");
```

Once a database is selected, `Execute` accepts DataVo SQL. The method returns a `List<QueryResult>` because a SQL string can contain more than one statement. Each `QueryResult` contains fields, row dictionaries, messages, and an `IsError` flag.

```csharp
db.Execute("""
CREATE TABLE Users (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  IsActive BIT
);
""");

db.Execute("INSERT INTO Users (Id, Name, IsActive) VALUES (1, 'Ada', true)");

List<QueryResult> results = db.Execute("""
SELECT Id, Name, IsActive
FROM Users
WHERE IsActive = true;
""");

QueryResult result = results[0];

foreach (var row in result.Data)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{row["Id"]}: {row["Name"]}");
}
```

For persisted local data, switch the same code to disk or LSM storage. Disk mode is the simpler file-backed mode. LSM mode is the high-throughput storage engine used in the headline benchmark results.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.Lsm,
    DiskStoragePath = "./datavo_lsm_data",
    LsmStrictFsync = true
});

db.Execute("CREATE DATABASE App");
db.Execute("USE App");
```

`LsmStrictFsync = true` is the conservative durability setting. It waits for the LSM write-ahead log to reach stable storage before acknowledging writes. Use relaxed LSM only for caches, rebuildable data, or benchmark runs where recent-write loss is acceptable.

## Lazy SQL Streaming (`StreamQuery`) and Live Views (`Subscribe`)

For large scans that should stream incrementally rather than buffering every row in memory, `DataVoContext.StreamQuery(sql, ...)` yields `DataVoRow` objects lazily over 1,024-row pages via `yield return` (short-circuiting cleanly on `LIMIT` or `break`). For continuous query updates without polling, `DataVoContext.Subscribe(sql, onChanged)` and zero-allocation `SubscribeZeroAlloc(sql, onChanged)` maintain Z-set deltas as data commits and drain on caller demand via `DispatchPendingNotifications()`.

See [Streaming Queries](/manual/client-interfaces/streaming-queries) and [Live Reactive Views (Z-set IVM)](/manual/client-interfaces/reactive-views) for API signatures, examples, and supported query shapes.

## Zero-Copy Table Streaming (`StreamRef` and `RowRef`)

For performance-critical loops (such as 60/120 FPS game simulation loops, real-time physics, or high-throughput batch pipelines), allocating C# heap objects per row creates GC pressure. DataVo provides `StreamRef()` on both `DataVoTable<T>` and `DataVoContext`:

```csharp
// Using a typed table
foreach (RowRef row in db.Table<Player>().StreamRef())
{
    int id = row.GetInt32(0);
    float health = row.GetFloat(1);
    ReadOnlySpan<char> name = row.GetStringSpan(2);
    // Zero bytes allocated on the managed heap!
}

// Or dynamically by table name
RowRefStream stream = db.StreamRef("Players");
int healthCol = stream.GetOrdinal("Health");
foreach (RowRef row in stream)
{
    float health = row.GetFloat(healthCol);
}
```

### Key Invariants of `RowRef`:
- **Zero Allocations:** On LSM and InMemory storage engines, a full table pass allocates 0 bytes on the managed heap (`GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() == 0`).
- **Direct Span Access:** Decodes primitive and string values directly in-place from storage memory spans (`ReadOnlySpan<byte>`).
- **Typed Accessors:** `GetInt32`, `GetInt64`, `GetFloat`, `GetDouble`, `GetBoolean`, `GetGuid`, `GetStringSpan`, `GetStringUtf8`, `GetVector3`, `GetVectorBytes`, `IsNull`, and `ColumnCount`.
- **Bounded Page Concurrency:** Reads rows in 1,024-row bounded pages, holding locks only during page block copies so concurrent writers and transactions are never stalled by reader loops.
- **Lifetime Safety:** `RowRef` is a `ref struct` scoped strictly to each loop iteration. To retain data across iterations, copy the values out of the span.

## Using Entity Framework Core

DataVo also includes an Entity Framework Core integration bridge (`DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore`). It is a preview bridge rather than a standalone EF provider: it attaches DataVo storage to an EF context while a host EF provider supplies EF's infrastructure services.

The example below uses EF Core's in-memory provider as that host provider, then registers DataVo with `UseDataVo`. The context derives from `DataVoDbContext`, which adds DataVo-specific loading helpers and query validation.

```csharp
using DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

public sealed class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public bool IsActive { get; set; }
}

public sealed class AppDbContext : DataVoDbContext
{
    public AppDbContext(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext> options)
        : base(options)
    {
    }

    public DbSet<User> Users => Set<User>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        modelBuilder.Entity<User>(entity =>
        {
            entity.ToTable("Users");
            entity.HasKey(static user => user.Id);
            entity.Property(static user => user.Name).HasMaxLength(80);
            entity.Property(static user => user.IsActive);
        });
    }
}

```

Register the context using normal EF Core options, then add `UseDataVo`.

```csharp
var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
    .UseInMemoryDatabase("datavo-ef-host")
    .UseDataVo(dataVo => dataVo
        .UseInMemoryStorage()
        .WithDataSource("App"))
    .Options;
```

You can then write through EF and query with ordinary LINQ for supported LINQ operators.

```csharp
using var ctx = new AppDbContext(options);

ctx.Database.EnsureCreated();

ctx.Users.Add(new User
{
    Id = 1,
    Name = "Ada",
    IsActive = true
});

ctx.SaveChanges();

List<User> activeUsers = ctx.Users
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(static user => user.Name)
    .ToList();

foreach (User user in activeUsers)
{
    Console.WriteLine(user.Name);
}
```

If data was written by another context session or directly through `DataVoContext`, call `LoadFromDataVo` before running EF LINQ so EF's change tracker mirrors the current DataVo tables.

```csharp
using var reader = new AppDbContext(options);

reader.LoadFromDataVo();

List<User> activeUsers = reader.Users
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .ToList();
```

For DataVo-native query evaluation, use `QueryFromDataVo`. This API validates the LINQ expression and either executes the supported subset or reports a clear unsupported-pattern error.

```csharp
List<User> firstTenActiveUsers = reader.QueryFromDataVo<User>(query => query
    .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(static user => user.Id)
    .Take(10));
```

## Entity Framework Core Support

The EF bridge supports basic `DbSet` querying (after data is written in the current context or loaded with `LoadFromDataVo`), basic inserts (`Add` plus `SaveChanges`), `QueryFromDataVo` for bounded `Where`, `OrderBy`, `Skip`, `Take`, and `Select` projections over mapped scalar properties, and vector LINQ shims (`CosineDistance`, `L2Distance`). Native EF-provider identity is planned. Migrations, shadow properties, complex joins, and broad `GroupBy` translation are **not** supported — unsupported grouped operators report unsupported-pattern errors.

---

# ADO.NET Provider (DataVo.Data)

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/ado-net
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/ado-net.md

`DataVo.Data` is a standard ADO.NET provider. Its types derive from the `System.Data.Common` base classes (`DbConnection`, `DbCommand`, `DbDataReader`, `DbTransaction`, `DbParameter`), so any code or library written against those abstractions can use DataVo without DataVo-specific adapters. That includes micro-ORMs such as [Dapper](/manual/client-interfaces/dapper).

```bash
dotnet add package DataVo.Data --prerelease
```

## Types

| ADO.NET base class | DataVo type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DbConnection` | `DataVoConnection` | Opens the embedded engine in-process. There is no network connection. |
| `DbCommand` | `DataVoCommand` | Text commands. Parameters use `@name` placeholders. |
| `DbDataReader` | `DataVoDataReader` | Forward-only reader over the command's results. |
| `DbTransaction` | `DataVoTransaction` | `Commit`, `Rollback` and savepoints. |
| `DbParameter` | `DataVoParameter` | `AddWithValue` is available on `DataVoParameterCollection`. |
| none | `DataVoConnectionStringBuilder` | Parses the [connection string](/manual/reference/configuration). |
| `Exception` | `DataVoException` | Carries `ErrorCode`, `Line` and `Column`. |

## Connect, create, insert, query

```csharp
using DataVo.Data;

using var connection = new DataVoConnection("StorageMode=Lsm;DataSource=./app-data");
connection.Open();

using (var create = connection.CreateCommand())
{
    create.CommandText = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Players (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(40), Level INT)";
    create.ExecuteNonQuery();
}

using (var insert = connection.CreateCommand())
{
    insert.CommandText = "INSERT INTO Players (Id, Name, Level) VALUES (@id, @name, @level)";
    insert.Parameters.AddWithValue("@id", 1);
    insert.Parameters.AddWithValue("@name", "Ada");
    insert.Parameters.AddWithValue("@level", 12);
    int affected = insert.ExecuteNonQuery(); // 1
}

using var query = connection.CreateCommand();
query.CommandText = "SELECT Id, Name FROM Players WHERE Level >= @min";
query.Parameters.AddWithValue("@min", 5);

using var reader = query.ExecuteReader();
while (reader.Read())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{reader.GetInt32(0)}: {reader.GetString(1)}");
}
```

`Open()` initializes the storage engine, creates the database named by `DataSource` if it does not exist, and selects it. `Close()` rolls back any open transaction and releases the engine.

## Transactions

A transaction is bound to the connection's session. `BeginTransaction()` starts it, and statements run on the same connection join it.

```csharp
using var transaction = connection.BeginTransaction();

using var update = connection.CreateCommand();
update.CommandText = "UPDATE Players SET Level = @level WHERE Id = @id";
update.Parameters.AddWithValue("@level", 13);
update.Parameters.AddWithValue("@id", 1);
update.ExecuteNonQuery();

transaction.Save("afterUpdate");   // SAVEPOINT
// ... more work ...
transaction.Rollback("afterUpdate"); // ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT

transaction.Commit();
```

Savepoints (`Save`, `Rollback(name)`, `Release`) are supported. For the isolation guarantees you can rely on, read [Transactions, ACID & MVCC](/manual/storage-engine/transactions-acid-mvcc). `DataVoTransaction.IsolationLevel` is reported for ADO.NET compatibility; the engine's documented contract is the source of truth, including its limits on predicate-level isolation.

## Prepared and parameterized commands

A command with parameters, or one on which you call `Prepare()`, runs through the engine's prepared-statement pipeline, so repeated execution does not re-parse the SQL.

```csharp
using var lookup = connection.CreateCommand();
lookup.CommandText = "SELECT Name FROM Players WHERE Id = @id";
lookup.Parameters.AddWithValue("@id", 1);
lookup.Prepare();

for (int id = 1; id <= 100; id++)
{
    lookup.Parameters[0].Value = id;
    object? name = lookup.ExecuteScalar();
}
```

## Errors

A failed statement throws `DataVoException`. Branch on `ErrorCode`, not on the message text. See [Error Handling](/manual/reference/error-handling).

```csharp
try
{
    insert.ExecuteNonQuery();
}
catch (DataVoException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{ex.ErrorCode} at line {ex.Line}, column {ex.Column}: {ex.Message}");
}
```

## Behavior to know about

- **The reader is forward-only over a materialized result.** `ExecuteReader()` runs the command and the reader walks the returned rows; it does not stream pages from storage. For zero-allocation streaming, use the typed table API, `RowRef` and compiled LINQ (see [Zero-Allocation Row Model](/manual/internals/zero-allocation-rows)).
- **Metadata is available before `Read()`.** `GetFieldType` and `GetName` work before the first row, as ADO.NET consumers expect. Column types are taken from the first non-null value in the result, so a column that is null in every row reports `object`.
- **Async methods run synchronously.** `ExecuteReaderAsync` and friends come from the `DbCommand` base class and complete on the calling thread; the engine is in-process.
- **`Cancel()` is a no-op and `CommandTimeout` does not cancel a running statement.** Lock waits are bounded by `LockAcquireTimeoutMs`; see [Configuration](/manual/reference/configuration).
- **One process owns a persisted database directory.** Connections in the same process that open the same directory share one engine and must use equivalent settings. A second process opening the directory gets `DatabaseInUseException`; see [LSM-Tree Engine](/manual/storage-engine/lsm-mode#opening-the-same-directory-twice).
- **There is no connection pool and no server.** Opening a connection is opening the engine.

## Native AOT

`DataVo.Data` builds with the trim and AOT analyzers enabled and the IL warnings treated as errors, so the provider itself is AOT-clean. If you add a reflection-based mapper on top, that library's AOT support applies. See [Native AOT Deployment](/manual/client-interfaces/native-aot).

## Related

- [ADO.NET & Dapper tutorial](/manual/tutorial/ado-net-and-dapper)
- [Dapper](/manual/client-interfaces/dapper)
- [Configuration Reference](/manual/reference/configuration)

# Dapper

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/dapper
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/dapper.md

Dapper works with DataVo through the standard ADO.NET provider. DataVo does not ship a Dapper-specific package or extension, and it does not need one: `DataVoConnection` is a `DbConnection`, and Dapper's extension methods operate on `IDbConnection`.

```bash
dotnet add package DataVo.Data --prerelease
dotnet add package Dapper
```

## Example

```csharp
using Dapper;
using DataVo.Data;

using var connection = new DataVoConnection("StorageMode=InMemory;DataSource=App");
connection.Open();

connection.Execute("CREATE TABLE Players (Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(40), Level INT)");

connection.Execute(
    "INSERT INTO Players (Id, Name, Level) VALUES (@Id, @Name, @Level)",
    new { Id = 1, Name = "Ada", Level = 12 });
connection.Execute(
    "INSERT INTO Players (Id, Name, Level) VALUES (@Id, @Name, @Level)",
    new { Id = 2, Name = "Linus", Level = 3 });

List<Player> strong = connection
    .Query<Player>("SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Level >= @min", new { min = 5 })
    .ToList();

Player? linus = connection.QuerySingleOrDefault<Player>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Id = @id", new { id = 2 });

int total = connection.ExecuteScalar<int>("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Players");

public sealed class Player
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public int Level { get; set; }
}
```

## Verified usage

The following calls have been run against `DataVoConnection` with Dapper 2.1.35 and behave as they do on other ADO.NET providers:

| Dapper call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `Execute` with anonymous-object parameters | Rows-affected count is correct. |
| `Query<T>` and `QuerySingleOrDefault<T>` | Rows map to POCOs by column name. |
| `ExecuteScalar<T>` | Returns the first column of the first row. |
| `QueryAsync<T>` | Works; it completes synchronously because the engine is in-process (see [ADO.NET Provider](/manual/client-interfaces/ado-net#behavior-to-know-about)). |
| `Execute` with an `IDbTransaction` | `Rollback()` discards the changes. |

Anything outside that list, such as multi-mapping, `QueryMultiple` and list parameter expansion, goes through the same ADO.NET surface but is not part of the verified set. Test those against your own schema before depending on them.

## Dapper or compiled LINQ?

| | Dapper | [Compiled LINQ](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Query language | Plain SQL strings | C# lambdas checked at compile time |
| Mapping | Reflection-based, per Dapper | Source-generated, no reflection |
| Allocation | One object per row, plus Dapper's own | Aggregates allocate nothing once warm |
| Native AOT | Governed by Dapper's own AOT support | Yes |
| Fits | Existing SQL, ad-hoc queries, joins | Hot-path lookups, filtered counts and aggregates |

The two coexist on one database: use Dapper for flexibility and compiled LINQ for the handful of queries that dominate your profile.

## Related

- [ADO.NET Provider (DataVo.Data)](/manual/client-interfaces/ado-net)
- [ADO.NET & Dapper tutorial](/manual/tutorial/ado-net-and-dapper)
- [Choosing an Interface](/manual/getting-started/choosing-an-interface)
