# Entity Framework Support

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/entity-framework
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/entity-framework.md

DataVo's Entity Framework Core integration (`DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore`) is a preview bridge. It helps EF users integrate DataVo with familiar `DbContext` and `DbSet` patterns, but it is not a standalone migration-capable EF provider.

The bridge expects a host EF provider for EF infrastructure services. In examples, the EF in-memory provider is a convenient host, and `UseDataVo` attaches DataVo-specific behavior.

The following example is a complete `Program.cs` for a small EF-backed DataVo evaluation. It defines the entity, declares the context, registers EF's in-memory host provider, attaches DataVo, writes one row, reloads DataVo state in a second context, and runs a supported LINQ query pattern.

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;

var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
    .UseInMemoryDatabase("datavo-ef-host")
    .UseDataVo(dataVo => dataVo
        .UseInMemoryStorage()
        .WithDataSource("EfDemo"))
    .Options;

using (var writer = new AppDbContext(options))
{
    writer.Database.EnsureCreated();

    writer.Users.Add(new User
    {
        Id = 1,
        Name = "Ada",
        IsActive = true
    });

    writer.SaveChanges();
}

using (var reader = new AppDbContext(options))
{
    reader.LoadFromDataVo();

    List<User> firstTenActiveUsers = reader.QueryFromDataVo<User>(query => query
        .Where(static user => user.IsActive)
        .OrderBy(static user => user.Id)
        .Take(10));

    foreach (User user in firstTenActiveUsers)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{user.Id}: {user.Name}");
    }
}

public sealed class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public bool IsActive { get; set; }
}

public sealed class AppDbContext : DataVoDbContext
{
    public AppDbContext(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext> options)
        : base(options)
    {
    }

    public DbSet<User> Users => Set<User>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
        modelBuilder.Entity<User>(entity =>
        {
            entity.ToTable("Users");
            entity.HasKey(static user => user.Id);
            entity.Property(static user => user.Name).HasMaxLength(80);
            entity.Property(static user => user.IsActive);
        });
    }
}
```

Use query capability checks before running a LINQ query that may be outside the supported bridge subset.

## Entity Framework Support Summary

Supported: basic `DbSet` querying over mapped scalar CLR properties, basic inserts (`Add` plus `SaveChanges`), `LoadFromDataVo`, `QueryFromDataVo`/`QueryFromDataVoAsync` (`Where`, `OrderBy`, `ThenBy`, `Skip`, `Take`, `Select`), `ExplainQueryFromDataVo` capability checks, and vector function shims (`CosineDistance`, `L2Distance`). Native provider identity is planned. **Not** supported: migrations, shadow properties, complex LINQ joins, and broad `GroupBy` translation.

---

# Roslyn Source Generators

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/source-generators
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/source-generators.md

Use source-generated queries for queries called often enough that parse and mapping overhead matters. Instead of parsing and planning the same SQL pattern repeatedly at runtime, you annotate a static partial method, or write a lambda against `DataVoTable<T>`, and the `DataVo.Generators` package emits the call path at build time.

`DataVo.Generators` is a Roslyn source generator and nothing more: it depends on the C# compiler APIs, not on Entity Framework Core, and the code it emits uses only `DataVo.Core`. That makes it the LINQ-shaped API to use in Native AOT applications and anywhere EF Core is unwanted. It compiles single-table `Where`, `Count`, `Any`, `Sum`, `Min`, `Max`, `FirstOrDefault`, `SingleOrDefault` and `ToList`, sorting with `OrderBy`/`OrderByDescending`/`ThenBy`/`ThenByDescending`, paging with `Skip`/`Take`, `Select` projections that read only the projected columns, and bulk `ExecuteDelete`/`ExecuteUpdate`. Shapes it cannot compile still return the right rows, in memory, and the build says why.

Start with a projection type.

```csharp
public sealed record PlayerProjection(int Id, string Name, int Level);
```

Then declare a static partial method with `[DataVoQuery]`.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.CompiledQueries;

public static partial class GameQueries
{
    [DataVoQuery("SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Id = @id")]
    public static partial PlayerProjection? GetPlayer(DataVoContext db, int id);
}
```

At runtime, call the generated method like ordinary C#.

```csharp
PlayerProjection? player = GameQueries.GetPlayer(db, 42);
```

The first parameter must be `DataVoContext`. SQL parameters such as `@id` must match C# method parameters after the context parameter.

```csharp
public static partial class PlayerWrites
{
    [DataVoQuery("INSERT INTO Players (Id, Name, Level) VALUES (@id, @name, @level)")]
    public static partial IReadOnlyList<long> InsertPlayer(DataVoContext db, int id, string name, int level);

    [DataVoQuery("UPDATE Players SET Level = @level WHERE Id = @id")]
    public static partial int UpdateLevel(DataVoContext db, int id, int level);
}
```

For indexed point lookups, provide a schema manifest as an additional file. The generator can use that manifest to pre-resolve single-column index hints.

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <AdditionalFiles Include="datavo.schema.sql" DataVoSchemaManifest="true" />
</ItemGroup>
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE Players (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(80),
  Level INT
);

CREATE INDEX IX_Players_Name ON Players (Name);
```

Use generated queries for stable point reads, inserts, and narrow fixed-shape updates. Use runtime SQL for exploratory queries, joins, aggregates, vector search, and complex SQL.

## Typed Table Queries

A model marked `[DataVoTable]` can be queried with lambdas through `DataVoContext.Table<T>()`. The generator reads each lambda when the project builds and replaces the call with a prepared statement, using C# interceptors. No expression tree is built, nothing is reflected over, and nothing is compiled at run time, so the calls are safe under Native AOT.

```csharp
[DataVoTable("players")]
public sealed class Player
{
    [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; }
    [Indexed] public int Level { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public bool IsActive { get; set; }
}

DataVoTable<Player> players = db.Table<Player>();

// Pass values as state and mark the lambda static: no closure, and the value goes straight to the statement.
Player? one = players.FirstOrDefault(targetId, static (p, id) => p.Id == id);

foreach (Player p in players.Where((min, max), static (p, r) => p.Level >= r.min && p.Level <= r.max))
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Name);
}

// Literals and constants need no state.
Player? admin = players.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Id == 1);
List<Player> veterans = players.Where(p => p.Level >= 50 && p.IsActive).ToList();
```

`FirstOrDefault`, `SingleOrDefault` and `Where` are available with and without state. `Where` returns a `DataVoQuery` that runs when it is enumerated and offers `FirstOrDefault()`, `SingleOrDefault()`, `Any()`, `Count()`, `Sum()`, `Min()`, `Max()` and `ToList()`. Its `IsCompiled` property tells you whether the generator compiled it.

A primary-key equality on an LSM database reads one row and allocates only that row. A miss allocates nothing.

Enumerating a query streams. Rows are read in pages of 1,024 and each model is built as the loop reaches it, so a `foreach` over 100,000 matching rows keeps about one page alive, not the result. `ToList()` is the way to ask for everything at once. Scans that were not compiled stream the same way. Some queries read their matches before enumerating, as `StreamQuery` does: a query inside a transaction, a condition with an equality on an indexed column (few rows, read through the index), and a condition the paged scan cannot apply, which today means `||`, a null test, or `!=` on a nullable column.

### Counting, Summing And Finding Extremes Without Building Rows

`Count()` and `Any()` on a compiled query do not build model objects when the condition reads only unindexed `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `bool` or `Guid` columns (comparisons, null tests, `&&`, `||`). The generator also writes the condition as a struct that reads those columns from the stored bytes, and the storage scan tests each row with it where the row is stored: nothing is copied out, and only the cells up to the last column the condition reads are located. Once warm, such a count allocates nothing on the LSM and in-memory engines, where enumerating the same 100,000 matches allocates about 22 MB, and it runs 6 to 20 times faster. The read lock is held for 4,096 rows at a time, so writers run between batches. Inside a transaction the rows are streamed instead, so the count includes the transaction's own writes.

```csharp
int rich = db.Table<Player>().Where(5_000L, static (p, gold) => p.Gold > gold).Count(); // 0 B
```

`Sum` works the same way. `DataVoQuery` has `Sum` for `int`, `long`, `float` and `double` selectors. When the query's condition is compiled into the scan and the selector is one non-nullable column of its own type (`p => p.Gold`), the generator adds that column up inside the same scan; the total stays in the scan's own variables and no row is built. Any other selector (`p => p.Gold * 2`, a nullable column, a widening cast) runs as written over the rows. An integer sum that leaves its type's range throws `OverflowException`; a `float` sum is accumulated as a `double` and rounded once, as LINQ does.

```csharp
long gold = db.Table<Player>().Where(static p => p.IsActive).Sum(static p => p.Gold); // 0 B
```

`Min` and `Max` are found in the same scan. `DataVoQuery` has `Min(selector)` and `Max(selector)` for any value type, with the semantics of `Enumerable.Min` and `Enumerable.Max`:

- Null values are skipped.
- When no row matches, or every value is null, the call throws `InvalidOperationException` for a type that cannot be null (`int`) and returns `null` for one that can (`int?`, `string`).
- A floating-point `NaN` orders below every number, so `Min` returns `NaN` if any value is `NaN`, and `Max` returns `NaN` only when every value is.

When the query's condition is compiled into the scan and the selector is one `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `DataVoDate` or `DateOnly` column of its own type, nullable or not, the generator keeps the smallest or largest value in the scan's own variables: no row is built and, once warm, nothing is allocated on the LSM and in-memory engines. Any other selector (`p => p.Gold * 2`, a cast, a `string` column) runs as written over the rows. Inside a transaction the rows are streamed instead of read in place, so the result includes the transaction's own writes.

```csharp
var active = db.Table<Player>().Where(static p => p.IsActive);
long poorest = active.Min(static p => p.Gold);          // 0 B; throws when no player is active
int? bestBonus = active.Max(static p => p.Bonus);       // 0 B; null when no active player has a bonus
DataVoDate first = active.Min(static p => p.JoinedOn);  // 0 B
```

DataVo has no `DATETIME` column: a `DateTime` property is not mapped, and a point in time is stored as a `long` (ticks or Unix time), which `Min` and `Max` read as any other `long` column.

The scan is generic over the compiled condition all the way into the storage engine's row loop, so no delegate is called per row.

When every column up to the last one the query reads has a fixed width (`int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `Guid`, dates), values sit at the same byte offset in every row whose leading cells are all present. The condition is then also compiled in a form that reads stored bytes at those offsets, worked out once per scan, with no row view built and no branch between its tests. Each row is first checked against that layout by its leading null flags. A row that differs, such as one holding a NULL in a leading column, is tested the general way, so results are identical. An in-memory table goes one step further. Its rows are separate objects, so the first compiled scan of a table writes each row once more as a short fixed-length record, a null flag and the value's bytes for every column, with text and vector columns keeping only their flag. The records lie side by side in large blocks, and later scans read those: memory is read in order, and every column sits at the same offset in every row, including rows with NULLs and tables with text columns ahead of the ones read. Scans keep the records up to date as rows are added and deleted. They cost a few dozen bytes per row, and only tables that are scanned this way have them. Put fixed-width columns before text columns in a model to get this path; a condition on a column that follows a `string` still runs in the scan, through the general reader.

On 200,000 rows with 100,000 matches a warm count, sum, minimum or maximum takes about 0.4 to 0.5 ms in memory, 1.7 ms on the disk engine and 2.0 ms on LSM (2.4 ms once flushed to an SSTable). Most of what remains on disk and LSM is the storage iteration itself.

A condition on the primary key or an indexed column keeps using the index, and a condition that compares text is evaluated by the SQL engine; both count by reading the matching rows, as before.

### Sorting And Paging

`DataVoTable<T>` and the `DataVoQuery` a `Where` returns have `OrderBy` and `OrderByDescending`; the sorted query has `ThenBy` and `ThenByDescending`. All of them, and the projections below, have `Skip` and `Take`. When every key is one column (`p => p.Column`, of the column's own type) and the filter is compiled, the engine sorts and pages the rows: the query becomes `ORDER BY ... LIMIT @limit OFFSET @offset`, and a `Take` after a sort keeps only that many rows while it scans instead of sorting the table.

```csharp
List<Player> page = db.Table<Player>()
    .Where(true, static (p, active) => p.IsActive == active)
    .OrderByDescending(static p => p.Level)
    .ThenBy(static p => p.Id)
    .Skip(pageIndex * 20)
    .Take(20)
    .ToList();
```

The results are the ones LINQ to Objects gives over the same rows:

- Each key orders by `Comparer<TKey>.Default`: null first when sorting up and last when sorting down, a floating-point `NaN` below every number, text in the current culture's order. Ties keep the order the unsorted query enumerates its rows in.
- `Skip` and `Take` follow `Enumerable.Skip` and `Enumerable.Take`: a count of zero or less skips nothing or takes nothing, and chained calls narrow one window (`Skip(2).Take(10).Skip(3).Take(4)` keeps rows 6 to 9). `Take(0)` does not run a statement.
- `Count()` and `Any()` on a sorted or paged query do not sort; they count the filter's matches (inside the scan when the filter is compiled into it) and apply the window. `FirstOrDefault()` reads one row and `SingleOrDefault()` two.
- Without `OrderBy`, `Skip` and `Take` page the rows in the order the query enumerates them, which is storage order for a scan. Sort first for a stable page.

A key the generator cannot compile (a computed key such as `p => p.Level % 7`, a cast, a `Vector3` column) sorts in memory, with the same result, and the build warns with `DATAVOL004`. An overload that takes a comparer always sorts in memory, without a warning. A sorted query also chains with `System.Linq`: `Enumerable.ThenBy` on it adds an in-memory key.

### Projections

`Select` on a table, a filtered, sorted or paged query projects each row. When the generator compiles the selector, the statement selects only the columns the selector reads (the engine still reads the filter's and the sort's columns to test and order rows) and the result is built straight from those columns: no model is built, so `Select(p => p.Name)` over a row with a large text column never decodes that text.

```csharp
public sealed record PlayerName(int Id, string Name);

List<string> names = db.Table<Player>().Select(static p => p.Name).ToList();          // SELECT Name FROM players
var board = db.Table<Player>()
    .OrderByDescending(static p => p.Score)
    .Take(10)
    .Select(static p => new { p.Name, p.Score, Rank = p.Score > 1_000 ? "gold" : "silver" })
    .ToList();                                                                          // SELECT Name, Score FROM players ORDER BY Score DESC LIMIT @limit
PlayerName? first = db.Table<Player>().Where(static p => p.IsActive).Select(static p => new PlayerName(p.Id, p.Name)).FirstOrDefault();
```

A compiled selector can build a scalar, a tuple, an anonymous type, a class or record through its constructor or an object initializer, a collection, or any expression over the row's columns, constants and accessible static members: arithmetic, `?:`, `??`, `?.`, `switch` expressions and patterns, interpolated strings, casts, and calls to methods, including extension methods such as `p.Name.Count()`. The projected query's `Sql` property shows the statement it runs, and `IsCompiled` says whether no model is built.

A selector that uses the row itself (`p => p`, `p => Describe(p)`), captures a variable or contains a lambda reads models and runs as written, and the build warns with `DATAVOL004`. A projection whose filter or sort runs in memory also reads models, since the filter and the keys need them.

### Reactive Subscriptions And Zero-Allocation Buffered Windows

Every `[DataVoTable]` table and composed LINQ query (`Where`, `OrderBy`/`ThenBy`, `Skip`, `Take`, `Select`) supports strongly-typed reactive subscriptions without writing SQL. See [Live Reactive Views (Z-set IVM)](/manual/client-interfaces/reactive-views) and [Choosing a Subscription API](/manual/client-interfaces/reactive-views#choosing-a-subscription-api) for the full comparison across all five reactive APIs:

- **`.Subscribe(Action<QueryChange<T>> onChanged)`** delivers strongly-typed `Added`, `Removed`, `Updated`, and `UpdatedBefore` collections whenever `db.DispatchPendingNotifications()` drains committed writes.
- **`.SubscribeInto(Memory<TProjection> destination, Action<int> onUpdated)`** writes the current live window directly into `destination.Span[0..count]` (clamped to `destination.Length`) and invokes `onUpdated(count)`. For compiled `.Select(...)` projections, `DataVo.Generators` emits a zero-allocation value-type `IReactiveRowProjector<TProjection>` struct reading reactive `RowRef` cells by constant ordinal, allocating **0 bytes** on the managed heap per drain in steady state.

```csharp
public readonly record struct HudSlot(int Id, int Score);

var hud = new HudSlot[3];
using var sub = db.Table<Player>()
    .Where(100, static (p, minScore) => p.Score >= minScore)
    .OrderByDescending(static p => p.Score)
    .Take(3)
    .Select(static p => new HudSlot(p.Id, p.Score))
    .SubscribeInto(hud.AsMemory(), count => UpdateHud(hud.AsSpan(0, count)));
```

Inside an explicit transaction the engine reads the transaction's view of the table: the committed rows its snapshot sees, the old versions of rows other sessions changed since it began, and its own uncommitted inserts, updates and deletes. A single-table projection still decodes only the columns it selects, filters on and sorts by, so a wide text column it leaves out is not decoded there either. The rows the transaction itself wrote are serialized once per query to be read the same way.

### Bulk Deletes And Updates

`ExecuteDelete()` deletes the rows a table or a filtered query holds and returns how many it deleted. A compiled filter becomes one `DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...` statement; the whole table is `DELETE FROM ...`.

`ExecuteUpdate` sets columns of those rows with one `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE ...` statement and returns how many rows changed. The setters are a lambda that chains `Set` calls; the generator reads it at build time and the lambda is never run:

```csharp
int paid = db.Table<Player>()
    .Where(static p => p.IsActive)
    .ExecuteUpdate(250L, static (set, reward) => set
        .Set(p => p.Gold, p => p.Gold + reward)   // Gold = Gold + @u0
        .Set(p => p.Guild, "veterans")            // Guild = @u1
        .SetNull(p => p.Bonus));                  // Bonus = NULL

int reset = db.Table<Player>().ExecuteUpdate(static set => set.Set(p => p.Level, 1));
```

- A value is a literal, the state argument or a field or property of it, an accessible static member, or null for a nullable column (`SetNull`, or a state value that is null at run time). Pass values as state with a `static` lambda, as with `Where`.
- A computed value (`Set(p => p.Column, p => ...)`) joins the row's columns and such values with `+`, `-` and `*`. Every column in it must have the target column's type. The engine evaluates it, in double precision for `FLOAT` and `DOUBLE` columns.
- The primary key cannot be set, and a column cannot be set twice.

Both methods take part in an open transaction, so a `ROLLBACK` undoes them, and outside one each is a single atomic statement. A statement that fails (a `NOT NULL` column set to null, for example) throws and changes nothing. The statements are prepared once per shape and run like any other prepared `UPDATE` or `DELETE`, so a filter on the primary key (`Where(id, static (p, k) => p.Id == k)`) changes one row through its key.

When the filter cannot be compiled (it captures a variable, for example) the rows are still changed correctly: their primary keys are read first, then one statement per key runs inside a single transaction (the caller's, when one is open), so the change is applied whole or not at all.

`ExecuteUpdate` has no in-memory form, since only the generator knows which columns the setters name. A call it cannot compile fails the build with `DATAVOL005`, which says why. On a compiler without interceptors, such as Unity's, the call throws `NotSupportedException`; use a prepared `UPDATE` statement there.

### Columnar Indexes

Mark the columns that analytical queries filter and aggregate on with `[Columnar]`. `Ensure…Table` then creates one columnar index for the table, named `cx_<table>`, over the marked columns (the same index as `CREATE INDEX ... USING COLUMNAR`; see [CREATE TABLE](/manual/sql-language/create-table)).

```csharp
[DataVoTable("players")]
public sealed class Player
{
    [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; }
    [Columnar] public int Level { get; set; }
    [Columnar] public long Gold { get; set; }
    [Columnar] public double Ratio { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
}

long gold = db.Table<Player>().Where(50, static (p, min) => p.Level >= min).Sum(static p => p.Gold); // 0 B
```

`Count()`, `Any()`, `Sum`, `Min` and `Max` on a compiled query are answered from the index when every column the condition reads, and the column the selector reads, is marked. The condition may use comparisons, null tests, `&&` and `||`. The results are the ones the row scan gives, including the `OverflowException` of an integer sum and the `NaN` ordering of `Min` and `Max`, and nothing is allocated. On 200,000 in-memory rows with 100,000 matches these take 0.03 to 0.09 ms, against 0.4 to 0.5 ms for the row scan; see [Benchmark Results](/manual/performance/benchmarks#with-a-columnar-index).

- `[Columnar]` applies to `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `bool` and date properties, nullable or not. On any other type, ensuring the table fails with an error that names the column.
- The index accelerates both `InMemory` and `Lsm` storage modes (legacy `Disk` mode accepts the attribute and falls back to reading rows). On `Lsm`, flushed rows persist in columnar segments inside SSTables and are scanned out-of-core in 4,096-row chunks with per-chunk zone-map pruning while only unflushed rows sit in memory; floating-point `Sum` on `Lsm` uses the row path so rounding matches row order.
- A query that reads a column outside the index, and any query inside a transaction, read rows, as described above.
- The index is a second copy of the marked columns and is written on every insert and delete, so mark the columns such queries use, not every column.

### What Is Compiled

| Lambda | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `p.Id == value`, `value == p.Id` | `Id = @p0`; a point lookup when `Id` is the primary key or is indexed |
| `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | The matching SQL comparison |
| `p.IsActive`, `!p.IsActive` | `IsActive = true`, `IsActive = false` |
| `p.Guild == null`, `p.Guild is not null` | `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL` |
| `a && b`, `a \|\| b`, parentheses | `AND`, `OR`, parentheses |
| `OrderBy(p => p.Level)`, `ThenByDescending(p => p.Gold)` | `ORDER BY Level, Gold DESC` |
| `Skip(n)`, `Take(n)` | `OFFSET @offset`, `LIMIT @limit` |
| `Select(p => new { p.Id, p.Name })` | `SELECT Id, Name`, and the result built from those two columns |
| `ExecuteDelete()` | `DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...` |
| `ExecuteUpdate(v, static (set, v) => set.Set(p => p.Gold, p => p.Gold + v))` | `UPDATE ... SET Gold = Gold + @u0 WHERE ...` |

A value can be a literal, a constant, the state argument, a field or property of the state (including tuple elements), or an accessible static field or property. Null follows C# rules, not SQL rules: a nullable column that holds null counts as different from a value in `!=`, and a state value that is null at run time is answered by running the lambda over the table.

### What Is Not Compiled

A call the generator cannot compile still returns the right rows. A filter reads the whole table and tests each row with the lambda, a sort key or a selector runs in memory, and the build reports why:

| Warning | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `DATAVOL001` | The lambda captures a local, a parameter or an instance member. Pass it as state with a `static` lambda. |
| `DATAVOL002` | The lambda uses something that has no compiled form: a method call, arithmetic, two columns compared with each other, or a value whose type differs from the column's. |
| `DATAVOL003` | The project has not enabled interceptors for the generated namespace, so no call is compiled. |
| `DATAVOL004` | An `OrderBy`/`ThenBy` key or a `Select` selector has no compiled form, so that step runs in memory over whole models. The message says why. |
| `DATAVOL005` | An `ExecuteUpdate` cannot be compiled (a captured value, a computed value outside `+ - *`, the primary key, interceptors not enabled). This is an error: the call has no other way to run. |

Silence a deliberate scan with `#pragma warning disable DATAVOL001`. A delegate created elsewhere and passed in is treated as a deliberate scan and is not reported.

### Enabling Interceptors

The `DataVo.Generators` NuGet package enables interceptors for you. A project that references the generator another way, such as a project reference, needs this property:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <InterceptorsNamespaces>$(InterceptorsNamespaces);DataVo.Generated</InterceptorsNamespaces>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Interceptors need the C# 12 compiler or newer. On an older compiler, such as Unity's, the same code compiles and returns the same rows but every query is a scan; use the generated `Get…ById` method or a prepared statement on hot paths there. Unity's compiler also has no module initializers, so call the model's `Ensure…Table` method before `Table<T>()`.

## Spatial Queries

A `System.Numerics.Vector3` property is stored as a `VECTOR(3)` column. `DataVoTable<T>` can then find rows by position:

```csharp
using System.Numerics;

[DataVoTable("ships")]
public sealed class Ship
{
    [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    [SpatialIndex] public Vector3 Position { get; set; }
}

DataVoTable<Ship> ships = db.Table<Ship>();

// Rows within 50 units of a point, the sphere's surface included.
foreach (Ship ship in ships.WithinRadius(station, radius: 50f)) { }

// Rows inside an axis-aligned box. The corners may come in either order.
List<Ship> docked = ships.WithinBoundingBox(minCorner, maxCorner).ToList();

// The five closest rows, nearest first.
IReadOnlyList<Ship> closest = ships.NearestNeighbors(player, k: 5);
```

| Method | How it runs |
| --- | --- |
| `WithinRadius(center, radius)` | Streams the table a page at a time. Each row's stored coordinates are tested before the model is built, so rows outside the sphere cost no model and the test allocates nothing. Distances are compared in double precision, so a point exactly on the surface is included even far from the origin. |
| `WithinBoundingBox(min, max)` | Streams like `WithinRadius`. A `BoundingBox3` overload is also available. The box's surface is inside. |
| `NearestNeighbors(target, k)` | Uses the column's Euclidean HNSW index when it has one: it fetches twice `k` candidates and ranks them by exact distance. Without an index, inside an explicit transaction, or with `exact: true`, it streams the table once and keeps the best `k`, so the answer is exact. Ties keep storage order. |

`[SpatialIndex]` (or `[Indexed]` on a `Vector3`) makes `Ensure…Table` create a Euclidean HNSW index named `sx_<table>_<column>`. HNSW is an approximate search: it can, rarely, miss a true neighbor. Pass `exact: true` when every answer must be exact. `WithinRadius` and `WithinBoundingBox` always read the whole table, because an HNSW index answers nearest-neighbor questions, not range ones.

When a model has more than one `Vector3` property, name the column: `ships.WithinRadius(center, 10f, column: "Spawn")`. A nullable `Vector3?` is supported, and a row whose position is null never matches.

`Spatial3` and `BoundingBox3` expose the same math for your own code: `Distance`, `DistanceSquared`, `DistanceSquaredPrecise`, `IsWithinRadius`, `Contains`, `Intersects`, `ClosestPoint`. None of them allocate. They use `System.Numerics`, which the .NET JIT compiles to SIMD instructions and which Unity's Mono and IL2CPP run as plain scalar code. In Unity, convert at the boundary: `new System.Numerics.Vector3(v.x, v.y, v.z)`.

A lambda that compares a `Vector3` column, such as `Where(p, static (s, p) => s.Position == p)`, is not compiled to SQL (`DATAVOL002`); it scans and still returns the right rows.

## SQL DATE Projections

The cross-target projection type for SQL `DATE` is `DataVo.Core.DataVoDate`. Generated `DataVoDate` and `DataVoDate?` properties call `GetDate` and `GetDateOrNull`. On modern .NET only, generated `System.DateOnly` and `System.DateOnly?` properties are explicit adapters and call `GetDateOnly` and `GetDateOnlyOrNull`.

## Source Generator Support Summary

The generator supports `static partial` methods whose first parameter is a `DataVoContext`, with SQL/C# parameter validation, and it emits compiled paths for equality `SELECT`, `INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...)`, and `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE ...`, plus typed projection mappers and single-column schema-manifest index hints. It supports `System.Numerics.Vector3` columns with `WithinRadius`, `WithinBoundingBox` and `NearestNeighbors` on typed tables. Its typed table queries compile single-table filters, sorting, paging, column-minimal projections, `ExecuteDelete` and `ExecuteUpdate`. They do **not** compile joins, grouping, `Distinct` or general vector search, and they are not a full LINQ provider — use runtime SQL for those shapes.

---

# Native AOT

> Source route: /manual/client-interfaces/native-aot
> Source file: manual/client-interfaces/native-aot.md

DataVo locks Native AOT compatibility across `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data`; this has held since the 0.2 packages and is checked on every change by `scripts/check-aot-baseline.sh`. Both assemblies enable .NET trim and AOT analyzers and treat `IL2026` and `IL3050` diagnostics as build errors.

For dynamic SQL, DataVo parses the runtime SQL string without reflection-based type discovery.

```csharp
using var db = new DataVoContext(new DataVoConfig
{
    StorageMode = StorageMode.InMemory
});

db.Execute("SELECT Id, Name FROM Users WHERE Id = 1");
```

For queries called often enough that parse and mapping overhead matters, prefer source-generated queries (`DataVo.Generators`). The generator turns a supported SQL pattern into generated C# code that avoids repeated parse and mapper setup while remaining completely trim- and AOT-safe.

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;
using DataVo.Core.CompiledQueries;

public sealed record PlayerRow(int Id, string Name, int Level);

public static partial class PlayerQueries
{
    [DataVoQuery("SELECT Id, Name, Level FROM Players WHERE Id = @id")]
    public static partial PlayerRow? GetPlayer(DataVoContext db, int id);
}
```

AOT-targeted applications can publish directly with `PublishAot=true`:

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -r osx-arm64 /p:PublishAot=true
```

EF Core has its own upstream AOT and trimming constraints. Treat DataVo's `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` bridge separately from `DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data` when publishing Native AOT binaries.

```csharp
var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
    .UseInMemoryDatabase("datavo-ef-host")
    .UseDataVo(dataVo => dataVo.UseInMemoryStorage().WithDataSource("EfDemo"))
    .Options;
```

## Native AOT Support Summary

`DataVo.Core` and `DataVo.Data` are locked and passing under Native AOT (`PublishAot=true`), including the C#-native embedded core, ADO.NET provider (`DataVoConnection`, `DataVoCommand`, `DataVoDataReader`), source-generated query paths (`[DataVoQuery]`), and zero-allocation `RowRef` readers. `DataVo.EntityFrameworkCore` depends on EF Core's runtime infrastructure and is **not** covered by the Native AOT guarantee.

---

# Zero-Allocation Row Model

> Source route: /manual/internals/zero-allocation-rows
> Source file: manual/internals/zero-allocation-rows.md

DataVo can read rows without creating managed objects for them. The mechanism is `RowRef`, a `readonly ref struct` that points at a row's stored bytes, and `RowRefStream`, which feeds `RowRef` values to a `foreach` loop one page at a time. Once a thread has streamed a table of a given shape, a full pass allocates zero bytes on the managed heap.

This page explains what that means, how to use it, and where it stops applying.

## The idea

A conventional database API materializes each row: a dictionary, an object array or a POCO per row. With 200,000 rows that is 200,000 allocations, and the garbage collector pays for them later.

`RowRef` skips that step. It wraps a `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` over the stored row and decodes a cell only when you ask for it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Storage["Stored row bytes<br/>(page buffer)"] -->|"byte span view"| RowRef["RowRef<br/>(ref struct, stack only)"]
  RowRef -->|"GetInt32(col)"| Cell1["int"]
  RowRef -->|"GetFloat(col)"| Cell2["float"]
  RowRef -->|"GetStringSpan(col)"| Cell3["char span view"]
```

Because `RowRef` is a `ref struct`, the compiler guarantees it lives on the stack. It cannot be boxed, stored in a field of a class, captured by a lambda or used across an `await`. That restriction is what makes it safe to point at memory that the engine reuses for the next page.

## Use it

```csharp
using DataVo.Core;

RowRefStream players = db.Table<Player>().StreamRef();

// Look column positions up once, before the loop: this call allocates.
int health = players.GetOrdinal("Health");

float total = 0;
foreach (RowRef row in players)
{
    if (!row.IsNull(health))
    {
        total += row.GetFloat(health);
    }
}
```

The same stream is available without a model type: `db.StreamRef("Players")`.

## Rules for `RowRef`

- **A row is valid only inside the iteration that produced it.** The stream reuses its memory for the next page. Copy any value you need to keep.
- **Spans follow the same rule.** `GetStringSpan` and `GetStringUtf8` return views into the row; copy the text out (for example `new string(span)`) if you need it after the loop body.
- **Accessors require the column's own type**, with lossless widening (`INT` through `GetInt64`, `FLOAT` through `GetDouble`). Any other type throws `InvalidCastException`.
- **A NULL cell throws `InvalidOperationException`.** Check `IsNull` first on nullable columns.
- **Column indexes follow table order**, which is the order of `CREATE TABLE` or of the properties of a `[DataVoTable]` model.

## How a pass behaves

- Rows are read 1,024 at a time. The read lock is held only while a page is copied out of storage, so a slow loop body never blocks writers.
- A pass sees every row that existed for the whole pass exactly once. A row written or deleted during the pass may or may not be seen.
- A schema change to the table during a pass stops it with `InvalidOperationException`.
- Inside an explicit transaction the stream reads through the query engine so it sees the transaction's own writes. **That path allocates.**

## What "zero allocation" covers

The claim is deliberately narrow, and the benchmarks are consistent with it:

| Operation | Allocation |
| --- | --- |
| Full `RowRefStream` pass, after warm-up on that thread | 0 B |
| Compiled `Count`, `Sum`, `Min`, `Max` over a filtered scan of 200,000 rows (see [Compiled Scan Kernels](/manual/internals/compiled-scan-kernels)) | 0 B per query, measured with BenchmarkDotNet's `MemoryDiagnoser` |
| Point lookup into a `Player` on LSM storage | 144 B (the row itself) |
| Point lookup into a `Player` on in-memory storage | 1,008 B, more than SQLite's 608 B |
| A `RowRefStream` pass inside a transaction | Allocates |

The numbers come from the [Benchmark Results](/manual/performance/benchmarks). Zero allocation applies to scans over `RowRef`, not to every API: building a `Player` per row allocates a `Player` per row.

## Native AOT

Nothing here uses reflection or code generation at run time. `DataVo.Core` builds with `IsAotCompatible` enabled and the IL trim and AOT diagnostics treated as errors, so a regression fails the build. See [Native AOT Deployment](/manual/client-interfaces/native-aot).

## Related

- [Compiled Scan Kernels](/manual/internals/compiled-scan-kernels)
- [Query Planner & Fast Paths](/manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths)
- [Compiled LINQ (Source Generators)](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators)

# Compiled Scan Kernels

> Source route: /manual/internals/compiled-scan-kernels
> Source file: manual/internals/compiled-scan-kernels.md

A typed table query such as `db.Table<Player>().Where(...).Count()` does not build an expression tree and does not interpret a predicate per row. The DataVo source generator reads the lambda while your project builds and replaces the call with generated code. For conditions over fixed-width columns, that generated code is a scan kernel that tests stored bytes in place.

This page describes how that works, what shapes are compiled, and what happens when a shape is not.

## Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Src["C#: players.Where(min, static (p, m) => p.Level >= m).Count()"]
  Src --> Analyzer["Roslyn incremental generator<br/>(DataVo.Generators)"]
  Analyzer --> Emitter["Emitter"]
  Emitter --> Intercept["Interceptor method<br/>[InterceptsLocation] at the call site"]
  Intercept --> Kernel["Condition struct<br/>(fixed-offset byte and cell tests)"]
  Kernel --> Scan["Storage engine row loop<br/>(In-Memory, LSM, Disk)"]
```

1. **Analyze.** The incremental generator finds `DataVoTable<T>` calls and parses each lambda. Only the pieces that can be expressed without running code are accepted: comparisons, boolean tests, null tests, `&&`, `||` and parentheses.
2. **Emit.** For each call site it writes an interceptor in the `DataVo.Generated` namespace, marked with `[InterceptsLocation]`, so the compiler routes that exact call to generated code. The emitted code uses members within C# 9.
3. **Compile the condition.** When the condition reads only unindexed `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `bool` or `Guid` columns, the generator also writes it as a struct. The storage scan calls that struct for each row, where the row is stored.
4. **Run.** The scan is generic over the condition struct all the way into the storage engine's row loop, so no delegate is called per row.

Nothing is reflected over or compiled at run time, which is why these calls are safe under Native AOT.

## What the kernel does

When every column up to the last one the query reads has a fixed width (`int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `bool`, `Guid`, dates), values sit at the same byte offset in every row whose leading cells are all present. The condition is then compiled in a form that reads stored bytes at those offsets. Offsets are worked out once per scan, no row view is built, and there is no branch between the condition's tests.

Each row is first checked against that layout by its leading null flags. A row that differs, such as one holding a NULL in a leading column, is tested the general way, so results are identical. In-memory tables are read the same way from their typed cells.

Put fixed-width columns before text columns in a model to get this path. A condition on a column that follows a `string` still runs in the scan, through the general reader.

## Aggregates

| Call | Compiled scan | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Count()`, `Any()` | Yes, for conditions on unindexed fixed-width columns | No model objects are built. |
| `Sum(selector)` | Yes, when the selector is one non-nullable column of its own type | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`. The total stays in the scan's own variables. Integer overflow throws `OverflowException`. |
| `Min(selector)`, `Max(selector)` | Yes, when the selector is one `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `DataVoDate` or `DateOnly` column | Null values are skipped. `NaN` orders below every number. |

Any other selector (`p => p.Gold * 2`, a cast, a text column) runs as written over the rows and allocates accordingly.

```csharp
long gold = db.Table<Player>().Where(static p => p.IsActive).Sum(static p => p.Gold);
long poorest = db.Table<Player>().Where(static p => p.IsActive).Min(static p => p.Gold);
```

Inside a transaction the rows are streamed instead of read in place, so the result includes the transaction's own writes and the call allocates.

## What is measured

On the [Benchmark Results](/manual/performance/benchmarks) (200,000 rows, half of them matching, one local run), the compiled aggregates allocate 0 B per query, against 504 B per query for SQLite and 1,137 to 1,169 B for DuckDB through ADO.NET. On file-backed storage DataVo's aggregates run 2.3 to 2.6 times faster than SQLite's. DuckDB, a multi-threaded column store, is faster than DataVo on these aggregates. Read the [Benchmark Results](/manual/performance/benchmarks) for the full context, including which numbers vary.

In memory, rows inserted through the typed batch API are kept as packed typed records and rows inserted through SQL as stored bytes. The compiled kernels read both through the same fixed-layout row images, and a local measurement over 200,000 rows found no gap: about 2.3 ns per row for typed-batch rows and 2.9 ns for SQL-inserted rows on a `Count`. SQL statements over typed-batch rows used to decode every cell of each packed row and ran at about 56 ns per row, against about 35 ns for SQL-inserted rows; they now decode only the columns the statement reads, about 28 ns per row (one local run, not a BenchmarkDotNet measurement).

## Not compiled

A call the generator cannot compile still returns the right rows. It reads the whole table and filters it with the lambda, and the build reports why (`DATAVOL001` to `DATAVOL003`; `DATAVOL004` and `DATAVOL005` cover sort keys, projections and `ExecuteUpdate`). Reasons include capturing a local variable, calling a method, doing arithmetic in the predicate or comparing two columns. A condition on the primary key or an indexed column keeps using the index instead.

The full table of supported lambda shapes and diagnostics is in [Compiled LINQ (Source Generators)](/manual/client-interfaces/source-generators#what-is-compiled).

## Related

- [Zero-Allocation Row Model](/manual/internals/zero-allocation-rows)
- [Query Planner & Fast Paths](/manual/storage-engine/query-planner-fast-paths)
- [Storage Modes](/manual/storage-engine/storage-modes)

# Benchmark Results

> Source route: /manual/performance/benchmarks
> Source file: manual/performance/benchmarks.md

This page reports measurements of DataVo 0.2.0-rc.3 against SQLite, DuckDB and LiteDB, taken on 12 November 2026 on one machine. It replaces the July 2026 (v0.1 alpha) page, whose numbers no longer describe the engine. The SQL text path has changed substantially since (v0.4); for SQL queries and filtered vector search, [DataVo vs SQLite](./datavo-vs-sqlite.md) has the current measurements, and where this page's [SQL over 1,000,000 rows](#sql-over-1-000-000-rows) section disagrees with it, that page is right. Several of them could not be reproduced, and one comparison it made was not valid. [What changed since July](#what-changed-since-july) lists these.

Every number below comes from a file in [`docs/public/benchmarks/2026-11-12/`](https://github.com/ArintonAkos/DataVo-DBMS/tree/master/docs/public/benchmarks/2026-11-12). The charts are generated from those files by `docs/scripts/generate-benchmark-plots.py`.

## Summary

| Claim | Evidence | Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DataVo answers a filtered `COUNT`/`SUM`/`MIN`/`MAX` over 200,000 in-memory rows 9 to 10 times faster than SQLite on the Apple M4 Pro, allocating nothing. On the x64 GitHub Actions runners the factor is 3.5 to 4.7. | [Part I](#filtered-aggregates), [Part III](#benchmarkdotnet-on-three-platforms) | Compiled LINQ query against SQLite through ADO.NET. |
| With a columnar index on the columns the query reads, DataVo answers the same in-memory aggregates 2.6 to 5.1 times faster than DuckDB held to one thread, allocating nothing. | [Part I](#with-a-columnar-index) | `Level`, `Gold` and `Ratio` marked `[Columnar]`; Apple M4 Pro only. |
| Without that index, DuckDB held to one thread is 1.2 to 2.8 times faster than DataVo in memory, and 3 to 8 times faster on file-backed row scans. With a columnar index, DataVo outperforms DuckDB on both in-memory and LSM storage (up to 8.9× faster). | [Part I](#filtered-aggregates), [Part I](#with-a-columnar-index) | Column store against row store and columnar index. |
| A primary-key lookup takes 52.1 ns (`49.3 ns` median, 56 B allocated) in DataVo's compact in-memory engine and 236 ns (144 B) on its LSM engine, versus 736 ns and 1,609 ns on SQLite (608 B) and 65–75 µs on DuckDB. | [Part I](#point-lookup-by-primary-key) | 100,000 rows, shuffled keys. |
| With a device flush per commit, DataVo and SQLite cost the same on the Mac (4.0 ms per durable update) and on the Windows runner (2.4 and 2.5 ms). | [Part II](#durability-what-an-fsync-costs), [Part III](#research-scenarios-on-linux-and-windows) | Both flush the drive's cache on every commit. |
| On the Linux runner, where a flush is cheap (about 0.1 ms), SQLite's durable update is 2.3 times faster than DataVo's (0.097 ms against 0.223 ms median). I have not profiled why. | [Part III](#durable-updates-and-thread-scaling) | GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner, one run. |
| Without that flush, DataVo (Relaxed) is 1.4 times faster than SQLite (WAL, normal) on serial updates and 1.95 times faster on a 12-thread mixed workload. | [Part II](#durability-what-an-fsync-costs) | Neither is power-loss durable. |
| When a query is kept up to date incrementally, DataVo is 179 times faster than DuckDB and 658 times faster than SQLite on a three-table join. On a single-table aggregate it is 1.1 times faster than SQLite. | [Part II](#streamed-risk-views-incremental-maintenance) | 50,000 insert-then-read iterations. |
| On 12 November, DataVo's SQL text path was about 2.6 times faster than SQLite on `GROUP BY` and on a join at 1,000,000 rows, and slower on `COUNT` with a filter, `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and range scans. Range scans have since become a seek (1.5–1.8 times faster than SQLite); the other two still favour SQLite. | [Part II](#sql-over-1-000-000-rows), [DataVo vs SQLite](./datavo-vs-sqlite.md) | LSM engine, prepared statements. |
| A 28-query SQL matrix over 1,000,000 orders (final v0.4 run, 17 November) maps where each engine wins: DataVo on key ranges (1.5–1.8×), index lookups (2.4×), `GROUP BY` with up to 1,000 groups (2.8–3.0×), inner and `LEFT` joins on integer keys (2.3–9.7×), columnar aggregates (5–14×) and filtered vector search; SQLite on `GROUP BY` over an indexed high-cardinality key (2.4×), unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` (1.4×), full scans with `OR`, `LIKE` or unindexed equality (1.1–1.3×), and the `LEFT JOIN` anti-join (1.2×). The first run found five queries where DataVo returned a wrong answer; all are fixed. | [DataVo vs SQLite: When Each Engine Wins](./datavo-vs-sqlite.md) | LSM Relaxed vs SQLite WAL `NORMAL`, prepared statements, every answer checked against an oracle. |
| On uniform random 1536-dimension vectors, exact Flat search is the right choice at 10,000 vectors: HNSW is no faster per query and finds 64% of the true neighbours. On clustered vectors HNSW is 8 times faster at 96% recall. | [Part II](#vector-search) | Both measured. |

## Test environment

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Machine | Apple M4 Pro, 12 cores, 48 GiB, local APFS volume |
| OS | macOS 26.3 (Darwin 25.3.0), arm64 |
| Runtime | .NET SDK 10.0.103, runtime 10.0.3, Arm64 RyuJIT |
| Code | Commit `7c0a931`. The engine is identical to `2d0dcb9`; the only difference is a type alias in the benchmark runners. |
| Comparison engines | `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` 10.0.0, `DuckDB.NET.Data.Full` 1.5.3, LiteDB (as pinned by the benchmark host), `sqlite-vec` 0.1.9 |
| Conditions | Language-server processes from an IDE were running in the background. No CPU pinning. One run per scenario unless a table says otherwise. |

These are single-machine measurements without confidence intervals, except in Part I where BenchmarkDotNet provides them. Parts I and II describe this machine. [Part III](#part-iii-platforms) repeats the suite on GitHub-hosted Linux, Windows and macOS runners and shows which results carry over. A difference of under about 20% between two engines in Part II should not be treated as established. The [methodology page](./methodology.md) lists what each benchmark controls and what it does not.

## Part I: The BenchmarkDotNet specification

`benchmarks/DataVo.Benchmarks` runs the same `players` table and the same questions through DataVo, SQLite and DuckDB. Each benchmark checks that all engines return the same answer before timing begins. The suite takes about 15 minutes.

```bash
dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/DataVo.Benchmarks -- --filter '*'
```

**Configuration.** "Memory" means DataVo `InMemory`, SQLite `:memory:` and DuckDB `:memory:`. "File" means DataVo's LSM engine with default settings, SQLite in WAL mode with `synchronous=NORMAL`, and a DuckDB database file. None of the file configurations flushes on every commit. SQLite and DuckDB are called through ADO.NET, and that cost is part of their numbers, as the cost of DataVo's own API is part of DataVo's.

DuckDB appears twice. `DuckDB` uses its default of one thread per core. `DuckDB 1 thread` is a separate database opened with `SET threads = 1`, which is how DataVo and SQLite run: one thread per query. To compare engines on equal terms, use the `DuckDB 1 thread` column.

### Filtered aggregates

This benchmark was run twice. The first table is DataVo as a row store, with no index on the columns read. The second, under [With a columnar index](#with-a-columnar-index), is the same benchmark after `Level`, `Gold` and `Ratio` were marked `[Columnar]`.

200,000 rows, half of them matching `WHERE Level >= @min`. DataVo runs a compiled LINQ query (`Where(...).Count()`, `.Sum()`, `.Min()`, `.Max()`). SQLite and DuckDB run a statement prepared once and read it with `ExecuteScalar`. Mean time per query in microseconds. DataVo allocates 0 bytes per query, SQLite 504 bytes, DuckDB about 1,150 bytes.

![Filtered aggregates over 200,000 rows](/benchmarks/bdn-filtered-aggregates.png)

| Query | Storage | DataVo, row scan | SQLite | DuckDB, 1 thread | DuckDB |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `COUNT(*)` | Memory | 386 | 3,695 | 137 | 203 |
| `SUM(Gold)` | Memory | 526 | 4,817 | 204 | 226 |
| `MIN(Gold)` | Memory | 525 | 4,607 | 201 | 269 |
| `MAX(Ratio)` | Memory | 503 | 4,955 | 418 | 417 |
| `COUNT(*)` | File | 1,973 | 4,543 | 245 | 270 |
| `SUM(Gold)` | File | 2,115 | 5,935 | 374 | 327 |
| `MIN(Gold)` | File | 2,136 | 5,377 | 360 | 346 |
| `MAX(Ratio)` | File | 2,267 | 5,656 | 716 | 564 |

The half-width of the 99.9% confidence interval is at most 3% of the mean for every DataVo and SQLite row, and at most 6% for DuckDB (its default-thread `MAX` in memory). The full tables, with error and standard deviation, are in the `bdn/` folder of the raw results.

**Reading the result.**

- In memory DataVo is 8.8 to 9.8 times faster than SQLite. On file-backed storage it is 2.3 to 2.8 times faster. These ratios are for the M4 Pro. On the x64 GitHub Actions runners the in-memory ratio is 3.5 to 4.7; see [BenchmarkDotNet on three platforms](#benchmarkdotnet-on-three-platforms).
- Held to one thread, DuckDB is 2.8, 2.6, 2.6 and 1.2 times faster than DataVo on `COUNT`, `SUM`, `MIN` and `MAX` in memory, and 8.1, 5.7, 5.9 and 3.2 times faster on files.
- DuckDB's extra threads do not help at this size. In memory its default mode is the same as or up to 48% slower than one thread on `COUNT`, `SUM` and `MIN` (I did not investigate why), and on files it ranges from 21% faster to 10% slower.

**Why DuckDB wins these.** DuckDB stores each column contiguously and processes it in vectors of 2,048 values. A query that needs `Level` and `Gold` reads only those two columns, and its inner loop runs over a dense array of one type. DataVo is a row store. Its in-memory engine keeps a packed image of each row, written the first time a compiled scan touches the table, and the scan reads rows in order without chasing objects. That removes the object-graph cost: DataVo's in-memory `COUNT` takes about 1.9 ns per row, where the previous revision of this page reported 1.3 to 4.0 ms for the same four queries, which is 6 to 20 ns per row. But each row's image still holds columns the query does not need, so the scan reads more bytes per row than a column store does. The 1.2 times gap on `MAX(Ratio)` is smaller than the others. The benchmark does not establish why; I have not profiled DuckDB's floating-point maximum.

On file-backed storage DataVo takes 4 to 5 times its in-memory time. The extra cost is iterating rows out of the LSM, not evaluating the query. DuckDB's file-backed times are 1.3 to 1.8 times its in-memory times.

This is a benchmark that plays to column stores. A workload that reads whole rows, or fetches one row at a time, reverses the ordering, as the next two benchmarks show.

#### With a columnar index

DataVo can keep chosen columns a second time as dense arrays of one type, beside the rows. The benchmark's model was changed to ask for that on the three columns these queries read:

```csharp
[Columnar] public int Level { get; set; }
[Columnar] public long Gold { get; set; }
[Columnar] public double Ratio { get; set; }
```

Nothing else changed: the same queries, the same rows, the same machine, SQLite and DuckDB as before. The index is opt-in. It is not something DataVo does by default, and DuckDB is columnar without being asked. The numbers below are a second run of the whole benchmark, so the SQLite and DuckDB columns differ slightly from the table above. Mean time per query in microseconds.

| Query | Storage | DataVo, columnar index | SQLite | DuckDB, 1 thread | DuckDB |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `COUNT(*)` | Memory | 27.5 | 3,915 | 141 | 188 |
| `SUM(Gold)` | Memory | 77.8 | 4,777 | 204 | 228 |
| `MIN(Gold)` | Memory | 73.0 | 4,598 | 200 | 258 |
| `MAX(Ratio)` | Memory | 89.5 | 4,996 | 421 | 417 |
| `COUNT(*)` | File | 27.5 | 4,730 | 246 | 294 |
| `SUM(Gold)` | File | 78.2 | 5,574 | 365 | 331 |
| `MIN(Gold)` | File | 73.4 | 5,393 | 362 | 358 |
| `MAX(Ratio)` | File | 90.1 | 6,051 | 740 | 554 |

DataVo allocates 0 bytes per query in every row of this table, SQLite 504 bytes and DuckDB about 1,150 bytes. The half-width of the 99.9% confidence interval is at most 2% of the mean for the DataVo rows. The full tables are in the `bdn-columnar/` folder of the raw results.

**Reading the result.**

- On both in-memory and LSM file-backed storage, DataVo with the columnar index is 2.6 to 8.9 times faster than DuckDB held to one thread (and up to 10.7 times faster than default DuckDB on `COUNT`), allocating 0 bytes.
- Against its own row scan in the first table, DataVo is 14 to 71 times faster.
- On the LSM engine the 200,000 rows of this benchmark fit in one MemTable and are never flushed, so these file-backed rows read the columns from the part of the index held in memory. Rows that have been flushed are read from the columnar segments of their SSTables instead; that is measured separately in [Columnar scans from SSTable files](#columnar-scans-from-sstable-files).
- This was measured on the Apple M4 Pro only, where the vector code runs as 128-bit NEON. The 256-bit and 512-bit forms are tested for correctness on every machine but have not been timed. The three-platform results in [Part III](#benchmarkdotnet-on-three-platforms) are the row scan.

**What it costs.** The index is a copy: 20 bytes per row for these three columns, about 4 MB for 200,000 rows, by the column widths (not measured). Every insert and delete also writes the index. I have not isolated that cost. The bulk load in this run took 42 ms with a standard deviation of 12 ms in memory, which is inside the noise of the load figures below, so the benchmark neither shows a slowdown nor rules one out. The point lookup did not slow down in that run: 335 ns in memory and 239 ns on a file (in-memory lookups were subsequently reduced to 52.1 ns after the compact row layout work below).

**How it works.** The index stores each column in chunks of 4,096 values, aligned to 64 bytes. A query's condition is run a chunk at a time: comparing `Level` with the bound value over a run of `int`s produces one bit per row, and the aggregate then reads only the `Gold` or `Ratio` values whose bit is set. No row is located or decoded, and the columns the query does not name are never touched. Comparisons, integer sums, minimums and maximums use vector instructions. A floating-point `SUM` is added one value at a time in row order, so it gives the same bits as the row scan. An integer `SUM` still throws `OverflowException` when it leaves the range of `long`. Readers take no lock; a query inside a transaction reads rows instead, so it sees the transaction's own writes.

The chart above shows the row scan.

### Columnar scans from SSTable files

Since v0.4 the LSM engine writes the indexed columns into every SSTable it flushes or compacts (format version 8), along with per-chunk `min`/`max` and `NULL`/`NaN` zone maps, and keeps in memory only the columns of rows that are not flushed yet. A columnar query skips non-matching chunks via their zone maps and reads surviving flushed rows a chunk of 4,096 at a time straight from the memory-mapped files, so opening a table builds no index and the memory used does not grow with the table.

`OutOfCoreAggregateBenchmarks` runs the four aggregates above over 1,000,000 rows on the LSM engine twice: with the rows not flushed (columns in memory) and after closing and reopening the database (every row in an SSTable, nothing of the table's columns in the managed heap). Apple M4 Pro, mean time per query in microseconds, 0 bytes allocated per query in every row.

| Query | Columns in memory | Columns in SSTable files |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `COUNT(*)` | 135.8 | 135.7 |
| `SUM(Gold)` | 388.9 | 388.2 |
| `MIN(Gold)` | 361.8 | 362.6 |
| `MAX(Ratio)` | 453.9 | 460.8 |

Opening the database, answering `SUM(Gold)` over the million rows from the files and getting the result takes 13.7 ms (186 KB allocated), with the files in the operating system's cache. The point lookup on the LSM engine measured 223 ns (144 B) in the same run, unchanged by the new file format.

**What this does not show.** The rows were inserted in key order and never updated, so no chunk needed a row masked out. A table with many updates or deletes since its last flush pays extra per query to find which rows of the files those replace; that cost has not been measured here. The files were in the page cache; a first read from a cold disk is not measured either.

### Point lookup by primary key

100,000 rows, keys looked up in shuffled order, each result read into a `Player`. DataVo runs a compiled LINQ query (`FirstOrDefault(id, static (p, k) => p.Id == k)`).

![Point lookup and bulk insert](/benchmarks/bdn-lookup-and-insert.png)

| Storage | DataVo | SQLite | DuckDB, 1 thread | DuckDB | DataVo alloc | SQLite alloc | DuckDB alloc |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Memory | 52.1 ns | 735.6 ns | 65,945 ns | 75,158 ns | 56 B | 608 B | 2,144 B |
| File | 236.0 ns | 1,609.4 ns | 64,877 ns | 72,314 ns | 144 B | 608 B | 2,144 B |

*Point lookup table measured on 13 November 2026 (`ce818d4`, after the v0.3 compact in-memory row layout) on the same Apple M4 Pro machine (DataVo in-memory median `49.3 ns`, error `±2.3 ns`). The chart above and the Bulk Insert section below reflect the earlier 12 November run.*

In memory DataVo is 14.1 times faster than SQLite (`1,267×` faster than single-threaded DuckDB) and allocates 10.9 times less managed memory (`56 B` vs `608 B`, where the `56 B` is the returned `Player` instance itself). On a file DataVo is 6.8 times faster than SQLite and about 275–306 times faster than DuckDB.

**Why DataVo is fast on the lookup path.** Three architectural properties explain the performance:

- *No SQL parsing or planning.* The source generator emits a static query plan (`PackedKeyReader<T>` for integer primary-key in-memory lookups, or cached prepared handles for other shapes).
- *No dictionary, scratch array, or boxing.* On compact in-memory tables, the source generator emits a direct `DataVoPackedRow` reader that decodes fields straight from the packed record bytes and reference slot into the target `Player` without allocating dictionaries or temporary `CellValue[]` buffers.
- *No lock on point reads.* LSM point reads go through a concurrent map of latest rows whose buffers are immutable once published. In-memory lookups probe the concurrent primary-key map and pack-store record without taking a table lock, re-checking row liveness after materializing reference fields so concurrent deletes never surface torn rows.

**What changed with the compact in-memory row layout.** An earlier revision of this page reported 405 ns (and before that 566 ns) for the in-memory point lookup and noted that it trailed the LSM file engine (`241 ns`). At the time, typed in-memory tables kept a `StoredRow` and `CellValue[]` array per row (~`640 B/row` retained for an unindexed row store with shared strings), and LINQ point lookups still routed through prepared-statement dispatch and a `Dictionary<string, object?>` (`~386.5 ns` on the pre-Option-C baseline). Storing fixed-width columns contiguously in `FlatRowStore` reduced row-store retained memory **13×** (`640.3 B/row` → `49.2 B/row` with shared strings; `145.3 B/row` with unique strings; `231.6 B/row` total including the primary-key index and unique strings), and pairing it with direct packed-record materialization dropped in-memory point lookup mean latency from `386.5 ns` to `52.1 ns` (`4.5×` faster than the LSM file engine).

SQLite's 1,609 ns (file) and 736 ns (memory) reflect the cost of B-tree descent plus the ADO.NET call, which allocates 608 bytes per lookup. DuckDB's roughly 65–75 µs is a fixed per-statement vectorization and pipeline setup cost: DuckDB executes statements through its vectorized chunk pipeline, which is optimized for multi-row analytical throughput rather than microsecond point lookups.

### Loading 100,000 rows

Into an empty table, with the rows built inside the measurement: DataVo's `InsertTypedBatch`, a prepared SQLite `INSERT` inside one transaction, and DuckDB's appender. Ten timed invocations per engine, so these are noisy; the standard deviation is shown.

| Storage | DataVo | SQLite | DuckDB, 1 thread | DuckDB | DataVo alloc | SQLite alloc | DuckDB alloc |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Memory | 35.0 ± 6.8 ms | 82.2 ± 37.2 ms | 28.7 ± 5.6 ms | 38.5 ± 4.9 ms | 55 MB | 94 MB | 19 MB |
| File | 133.4 ± 35.4 ms | 76.8 ± 26.5 ms | 31.1 ± 5.9 ms | 29.0 ± 5.8 ms | 62 MB | 94 MB | 19 MB |

Plus-or-minus values are standard deviations of ten invocations. In memory DataVo and DuckDB are within each other's noise, and both have a lower mean than SQLite, whose spread is wide. On a file DuckDB is 2.6 to 4.6 times faster than the two row stores. DataVo's file-backed load took 84 ms in an earlier run of this suite on the same day and 133 ms in this one. With a standard deviation of 35 ms the ordering of DataVo and SQLite on files is not established, and I do not claim one. DuckDB allocates the least, presumably because its appender copies rows into native memory.

## Part II: Real-world systems workloads

These scenarios come from `demos/Research.Benchmark`. They are closer to application workloads than Part I and have less statistical control: one run each, with latency percentiles computed over the run. Each scenario states which engines run which API. DataVo scenarios use typed APIs and prepared compiled queries after the schema is created, except where noted, so the SQL shown documents the logical workload and not necessarily the call that ran.

### Streamed risk views: incremental maintenance

A betting-risk dashboard needs an aggregate that is correct after every incoming order. Each iteration inserts one order and then reads the dashboard result. DataVo subscribes to the exact SQL once and reads the incrementally maintained view. SQLite and DuckDB re-run the full indexed query after every insert, with no trigger and no hand-maintained summary table.

This is a statement about two designs, not only two speeds. DataVo's read returns state that was updated as part of the insert. The polling engines recompute it. It also applies only to the query shapes DataVo can maintain incrementally. Anything else falls back to normal execution.

**Profile A, simple exposure.** `SELECT ... SUM(Stake) ... WHERE IsOpen = true GROUP BY MarketId, RunnerId` over a single table. 10,000 baseline orders, then 50,000 iterations.

| Engine | Total (ms) | P50 | P99 | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo | 526.9 | 6.4 µs | 21.3 µs | 364.6 MB |
| SQLite | 574.1 | 8.9 µs | 24.6 µs | 200.7 MB |
| DuckDB | 52,954.0 | 983 µs | 3,311 µs | 208.3 MB |

I repeated this scenario three more times for DataVo and SQLite. DataVo took 507 to 527 ms in all four runs and SQLite 574 to 753 ms.

![Streamed risk, simple exposure](/benchmarks/ivm-simple-exposure-total-time.png)

On this profile DataVo is 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than SQLite, which is a small margin. It also allocates 1.8 times as much managed memory, about 7.3 KB per iteration, so it is not an allocation win here. SQLite's indexed recompute stays under 15 µs per iteration at this scale; I did not examine its query plan. DuckDB's 983 µs median looks like a per-query fixed cost, consistent with its roughly 75 µs point lookups in Part I plus scheduling a parallel query, but I did not profile it.

July's version of this page reported SQLite at 2,820 ms, five times slower than today's figure. The SQLite runner has not changed since, and I cannot reproduce the July number. I do not know whether the cause was different hardware or a loaded machine, so I have not used it.

**Profile B, complex VIP exposure.** `SELECT m.Category, SUM(o.Stake) FROM Orders o JOIN Accounts a ... JOIN Markets m ... WHERE a.IsVip = true GROUP BY m.Category`. 10,000 baseline orders, 1,000 accounts, 50 markets, then 50,000 iterations.

| Engine | Total (ms) | P50 | P99 | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo | 191.7 | 3.1 µs | 4.0 µs | 106.6 MB |
| DuckDB | 34,339.1 | 660 µs | 974 µs | 131.3 MB |
| SQLite | 126,064.4 | 2,527 µs | 4,375 µs | 115.6 MB |

![Streamed risk, complex VIP exposure](/benchmarks/ivm-complex-vip-total-time.png)

DataVo is 179 times faster than DuckDB and 658 times faster than SQLite. The gap is large because of what each engine does per iteration. The polling engines join the whole `Orders` table against two dimension tables and aggregate it, and `Orders` grows from 10,000 to 60,000 rows during the run, so their per-iteration cost grows with the table. DataVo applies only the new order: it looks up the order's account and market, and if the account is VIP it adds the stake to that category's total. That work does not depend on how many orders already exist. SQLite's 2.5 ms median is the cost of a three-table join over tens of thousands of rows. DuckDB's parallel execution handles the same join in 0.66 ms, but it pays its fixed per-query overhead on top.

### Durability: what an fsync costs

`disk-crud-wal` inserts 20,000 records and then runs 20,000 point updates, committing each update separately.

| Engine | Total (ms) | P50 | P99 | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo (LSM Production) | 84,616 | 4.04 ms | 6.13 ms | 30.8 MB |
| SQLite (WAL, full, `fullfsync`) | 84,857 | 4.04 ms | 6.08 ms | 22.3 MB |
| DataVo (LSM Relaxed) | 113 | 4.5 µs | 7.5 µs | 22.9 MB |
| SQLite (WAL, normal) | 155 | 5.4 µs | 9.2 µs | 23.2 MB |

![Disk CRUD total time](/benchmarks/disk-crud-wal-time.png)

The two durable engines are indistinguishable: about 4.2 ms per update including the insert phase, and a median of 4.04 ms for the update alone. That is the cost of making one commit reach stable storage on this SSD, and neither engine can avoid it. The 750-fold gap between durable and non-durable DataVo is the price of that guarantee, not an inefficiency. The SQLite run sets `PRAGMA fullfsync=1`, so both engines ask the drive to flush its cache.

Without the flush, DataVo (Relaxed) and SQLite (WAL, normal) differ by 1.4 times in DataVo's favour on this serial workload, and the median and P99 latencies are within 1.2 times of each other. Relaxed mode acknowledges a write after it reaches the operating system's buffer. A power loss or kernel crash can lose the most recent writes. Use it for caches, rebuildable data and research, not as a substitute for the durable mode.

**Group commit.** When several threads commit at the same time they can share one flush. `thread-scaling` runs 100,000 reads and 10,000 updates at 1 to 32 threads:

![Thread scaling](/benchmarks/thread-scaling-throughput.png)

| Threads | DataVo Production | DataVo Relaxed | SQLite (WAL, normal) | LiteDB |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 2,686 | 1,333,227 | 335,281 | 49,027 |
| 2 | 2,962 | 1,276,043 | 559,224 | 68,793 |
| 4 | 5,506 | 1,101,274 | 589,921 | 68,873 |
| 8 | 8,777 | 1,025,118 | 577,691 | 67,864 |
| 16 | 9,550 | 1,028,862 | 569,653 | 65,402 |
| 32 | 9,840 | 1,011,191 | 555,357 | 66,020 |

Operations per second. Durable DataVo scales 3.7 times from one to 32 threads, which is consistent with concurrent writers sharing each flush (I did not count flushes). Relaxed DataVo does not scale: throughput falls 24% from one thread to 32. The whole run takes 83 to 109 ms, so thread start-up is a visible share of it. I have not profiled where the lost throughput goes. The machine has 12 cores, so 16 and 32 threads are oversubscribed. SQLite benefits from concurrent readers in WAL mode and reaches its peak at four threads. SQLite's durable (`full`) mode is not in this table, so the durable DataVo row has no like-for-like comparison here.

**YCSB mixed.** 100,000 preloaded records, then 80,000 reads and 20,000 updates across 12 threads.

![YCSB write P99](/benchmarks/ycsb-write-p99.png)

| Engine | Total (ms) | Ops/s | Read P99 | Write P99 | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo (LSM Relaxed) | 195.8 | 510,695 | 0.9 µs | 0.66 ms | 34.7 MB |
| SQLite (WAL, normal) | 382.2 | 261,618 | 8.2 µs | 3.77 ms | 57.2 MB |
| LiteDB | 2,640.1 | 37,877 | 2.59 ms | 2.79 ms | 4,315.1 MB |
| DataVo (LSM Production) | 23,118.6 | 4,326 | 25.7 µs | 27.83 ms | 37.2 MB |

DataVo Relaxed has 1.95 times SQLite's throughput, 5.7 times lower write P99 and 9.3 times lower read P99. The read result follows from the lock-free LSM read path described above: readers do not queue behind writers. The write P99 of the durable row, 27.8 ms, is what 20,000 flushes cost when 12 threads queue for them. Compare Production only with other durable engines.

### Space and cold open

1,000,000 records of `(Id INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(40), Value INT, Score FLOAT)`, inserted in one batch, closed cleanly and reopened.

| Engine | Insert (ms) | Disk (MB) | Reopen (ms) | First read after reopen (ms) | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo (LSM Production) | 731.8 | 27.7 | 4.3 | 3.6 | 400.7 MB |
| DataVo (LSM Relaxed) | 473.2 | 27.7 | 1.5 | 0.0 | 332.9 MB |
| SQLite (WAL, normal) | 712.5 | 29.1 | 0.36 | 1.2 | 633.4 MB |
| LiteDB | 2,987.1 | 154.5 | 0.61 | 9.4 | 15,107.2 MB |

DataVo's file is 5% smaller than SQLite's and 5.6 times smaller than LiteDB's. A million rows insert in 473 to 732 ms. The 258 ms difference between Production and Relaxed is consistent with Production flushing the log before acknowledging the batch. I did not count flushes, but a per-row flush would take minutes, so it is at most a few per batch.

**What the reopen figure does and does not mean.** This is a clean-close reopen inside the same process, immediately after the files were written, so the operating system's page cache is warm. It is not a measurement of recovery after a crash, and it is not a cold-cache boot. It shows that opening an LSM database does not read the data: DataVo maps its SSTables and loads their indexes, which takes 1.5 to 4.3 ms for a million rows. SQLite opens a file faster, in 0.36 ms, because it reads only the header and a few pages. The time to the first answer is 7.9 ms for DataVo Production, 1.5 ms for DataVo Relaxed and 1.6 ms for SQLite. Crash recovery, meaning replaying a write-ahead log after a hard stop, is covered by the crash-injection tests in `DataVo.Tests`, not by this benchmark.

### Vector search

10,000 vectors of 1,536 dimensions (uniform random components in [-1, 1], normalised), then 100 top-10 queries. The query vectors are existing vectors from the set, so each query's nearest neighbour is itself. Insert, index build and queries are all inside the total time. The SQLite row uses `sqlite-vec` 0.1.9; it is an exact brute-force scan.

![Vector search total time](/benchmarks/vector-search-total-time.png)

| Engine | Total (ms) | Query P50 | Query P99 | GC allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DataVo-Flat | 298.7 | 1.96 ms | 2.41 ms | 61.7 MB |
| SQLite (`sqlite-vec`) | 472.8 | 2.37 ms | 2.43 ms | 63.4 MB |
| DataVo (HNSW) | 1,634.0 | 1.77 ms | 2.25 ms | 62.8 MB |
| DataVo (HNSW, diversity heuristic) | 6,682.1 | 1.78 ms | 1.93 ms | 61.7 MB |
| LiteDB | 76,706.5 | 747.4 ms | 778.0 ms | 208,914.6 MB |

**What the GC column does and does not say.** The 61.4 MB that every DataVo and SQLite row shares is the vector data itself: 10,000 vectors of 6,144 bytes. This is one copy of the input made during insert. It is not a measure of search overhead. DataVo-Flat allocated 10.3 MB in the July run and allocates 61.7 MB now. I measured the commit before today's row-image change and got the same 62 MB, so that change is not the cause, and I did not bisect further. The July figure is not reproducible on the current engine, and the previous page's "10.3 MB" claim is withdrawn. LiteDB's 208,915 MB is 3,400 times the size of the input, which is consistent with deserialising every stored document, with its 1,536 floats, on every query. I did not profile it.

**Why Flat is the right choice at 10,000 uniform random vectors.** Three measurements support this, and the first two are in the table above.

1. *Build cost.* Flat builds nothing. Total time is 5.5 times lower than HNSW's.
2. *Query cost.* On this data HNSW queries are not meaningfully faster: 1.77 ms median against 1.96 ms. A Flat query costs about 196 ns per 1,536-dimension distance times 10,000 vectors. The HNSW query takes about as long, which means it evaluates distances for most of the graph. I inferred this from timing and did not count the evaluations.
3. *Quality.* Flat is exact. The table above does not show HNSW's recall, so I measured it separately with held-out queries, where a query's own vector is not in the set (`vector-recall-experiment.txt`, reproducible with `demos/Research.Benchmark/tools/VectorRecall`):

![HNSW versus Flat](/benchmarks/vector-hnsw-vs-flat.png)

| N | Data | Flat query | HNSW query | HNSW recall@10 | HNSW build | Flat build |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1,000 | uniform | 0.24 ms | 0.45 ms | 99.9% | 238 ms | 27 ms |
| 10,000 | uniform | 2.06 ms | 1.92 ms | 63.5% | 1,169 ms | 135 ms |
| 50,000 | uniform | 10.1 ms | 3.0 ms | 23.8% | 10,414 ms | 162 ms |
| 1,000 | clustered | 0.24 ms | 0.31 ms | 100% | 63 ms | 10 ms |
| 10,000 | clustered | 2.00 ms | 0.25 ms | 95.9% | 548 ms | 34 ms |
| 50,000 | clustered | 10.3 ms | 0.68 ms | 90.2% | 5,658 ms | 236 ms |

Uniform random vectors in 1,536 dimensions are the worst case for a graph index. Pairwise distances concentrate around one value, so the graph offers no useful direction toward a query's neighbours. HNSW with its default `EfSearch` of 64 then either explores most of the graph or misses neighbours, and at 10,000 vectors it does a bit of both: recall is 63.5%. Real embeddings are clustered, and the clustered rows show what happens then: HNSW answers a 10,000-vector query 8 times faster than Flat at 96% recall, and 15 times faster at 50,000. Its 514 ms of extra build time at 10,000 clustered vectors pays for itself after about 290 queries.

**Since 15 November** HNSW's diversity heuristic is on by default; the "DataVo (HNSW)" rows above ran without it. On strongly clustered data the old default left some queries with no correct result at any search width, and on uniform data the heuristic now costs 8–11% more build time rather than four times. See [HNSW on this data](./datavo-vs-sqlite.md#hybrid-vector-and-sql) in the SQLite guide.

So the claim that holds is narrower than "Flat beats HNSW up to 10,000 vectors": Flat wins at that size for the benchmark's random data, and for any workload that builds the index and runs few queries. For clustered embeddings that serve many queries, HNSW wins at 10,000 vectors as well. Flat's query time grows linearly, 0.24 ms, 2.0 ms and 10 ms at 1,000, 10,000 and 50,000 vectors, so for latency-sensitive workloads the crossover comes sooner than 10,000. Measure with your own embeddings. The recall experiment above is a template.

### SQL over 1,000,000 rows

`sql-workload` runs the operations of a small application through SQL text with prepared statements, against a million-row orders table in file-backed engines (DataVo LSM without a flush per commit, SQLite WAL `NORMAL`, DuckDB default, LiteDB default). Single-step rows show total time; repeated rows show the median and P99 of one call.

| Operation | DataVo | SQLite | DuckDB | LiteDB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
